this single page from Livermore > entire books that have been written 

1. “After spending many years in Wall Street and after making and losing millions of dollars I want to tell you this: It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. It always was my sitting. Got that? My sitting tight! It is no trick at all to be right on the market. You always find lots of early bulls in bull markets and early bears in bear markets.”

2. “I've known many men who were right at exactly the right time, and began buying or selling stocks when prices were at the very level which should show the greatest profit. And their experience invariably matched mine that is, they made no real money out of it. Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon.”

3. “In a bull market your game is to buy and hold until you believe that the bull market is near its end.”

4. “One of the most helpful things that anybody can learn is to give up trying to catch the last eighth or the first.”

quotedTweet.text:
Druck - 8 incredible excerpts/masterclass on literally everything - risk, concentration, traits of great traders - from 2009 intvw with Jeff Feig (ht @kevg1412)

1. Druck on getting his start in the business

"You couldn't sell snowmobiles in Alaska if there was no other transportation vehicle there."

"And I got a job in construction. And then the only job I could get was at Pittsburgh National. And I started in the training program. In a bank, you're a teller, you go through the credit department, and everybody wants to go to the credit department. And I thought I was pretty smart. There were 12 of us. I had a pretty high opinion of myself, and I went in after we went through the training program, and the guy at credit said, You couldn't sell snowmobiles in Alaska if there was no other transportation vehicle there. So we have no use for you anywhere in the bank. But there's a guy up on the 30th floor whose personality is worse than yours, who runs the trust department. He's a great investor--you should call him up and see if he'll hire you. So I called the guy up and he said, Where'd you go to school? And I said, I met University of Michigan. And before I get out--he said, I went to Michigan. You're hired."

2. On charts, and fundamentals vs. technicals:

Okay, so every night, at about 4:30, I get 272 charts. They cover just about every group in the stock market, every commodity, every currency cross I'm interested, in every fixed income market around the world. And they're basically daily, weekly, and monthly. Daily supposed to predict 8-20 days, weekly 8-20 weeks, and monthly 8-20 months. When I make an investment decision, it's usually--sometimes, believe it or not: The idea comes from the charts, but I will never invest just on a chart. But if I really like a fundamental thesis and the chart stinks, I won't do it.

3. On Concentration

"So I went into him, and I said, George, I just want you to know I'm going to do $5bn worth of the pound. I don't think I had told him about the $1.5bn. I've been monitoring this for a while. I went through the thesis, and the whole economic pitch I gave you. And he goes, That's ridiculous. And I said, Excuse me? George, this is like a layup. He says, Exactly the point. Why are you only doing $5bn? So he says, This is a one way bet. It's not the way you manage risk. You should do $15bn, because the forwards are still, like 0.5-0.75%."

4. On Concentration (cont)

But you ask a great question, because--and this is not something I did, but this is a great trading lesson. I wasn't there, but [Oaken (ph)] will tell you the story, because he was. And this is a great investor--his name is George Soros. And when Plaza happened in '85, he was loaded to the brink with Yen--like, already too big. And all the little traders there--we didn't have this when I was running Quantum, but they had their little $25-50mn capital pools.

They were allowed to piggyback, so they were all long Yen, because, frankly, George was long Yen. So the next morning, after Plaza, the Yen opened up 800 ticks.

And George Soros is an interesting guy, but I worked for him for 12 years, and I never heard him swear, and I never saw much emotional change. Takes--that lasted me for about four minutes, if you were with me on a desk. But apparently, all these other guys started taking profits, and he had an absolute heart attack.

Stop it. Transfer all that stuff to me. They're idiots!

And the thing went another 40%--another 4,000 ticks. So the easy thing emotionally was to take a profit. And in fact, George was adding, and taking that too, because you can't just make yourself feel good by taking a profit when something goes your way. You have to remember your original game plan, your original thesis, and why you thought it would go from, if it's A to B, wherever B is.

5. Druck on stops - "I have them"

Yeah, I have never used a stop loss in my career. I don't use a--like a number. I know that's a disciplined system and I know it works, but I have like conditions: if it starts not acting well relative to news or other things I'm watching, I'll get out. So I probably do have a stop loss in my head.

6. Traits of great traders

Jeff Feig: So what is it you think that makes a good trader? I mean, I know you got a lot of friends who are pretty legendary traders, all with different styles. You've had a lot of people work for you, people that you've worked for. What is the common denominator?

Stan Druckenmiller: Well, I'd say first of all, they're extremely competitive. They want--they have an unbelievable will to win. And that just--if you look at anybody with a great investment record, for whatever reason, the people without passion can't compete with them, because they have passion, and they're willing to just work--work harder. And you're in the wrong arena if you think you can compete with those maniacs if you don't have that passion. 

Number two: they may have very, very different styles, but they're all disciplined. And I just told you about four times I wasn't disciplined. But that's over about 30 years. It doesn't even matter what your system is, but as long as you follow it, there are a lot of ways to make money. And with regards to that, you really, really have to fight your emotions. Because I have wanted to sell every bottom so bad. And a lot of times I'm buying there. I'm always doing--it never feels great when you're at a turn. 

The other thing I have found is that contrarian investing is way overrated. People tend to--it's intellectually cool to not be with the crowd, but the crowd makes money 80% of the time. And they kill themselves at the turns and end up losing as much as the turns as they make during the 80% of the time. But I have found contrarian thinking, just to be contrarian, can be a death trap, particularly in bonds and currencies, because economic fundamentals are what they are. It can be a rough ride if it's very crowded. 

But I think the main thing, Jeff, is you have to be disciplined. You have to be unemotional. And to me, the really great ones--you have to really be able to play. You have to have courage. You have to play big when the opportunity is there--make hay while the sun shines, whatever the term is.

7. On risk systems

Stan Druckenmiller: I don't remember when you walked in, but this is a terrific question, because I have never had a--well I did, but I didn't pay attention to it, and it's what Tom's alluding to--I have never had a fancy quantitative risk management control system overseeing me. And by the way, neither did George Soros in the 25 years he ran the fund before I did. And between us, there's one down year since 1969.

8. On P&L-watching as the best risk system

But when you really, really need risk management, they break down. Because by definition of a financial crisis, which I'm sure everybody here knows, because we had a recent one, correlations just go wacko. The stuff that has correlated for years breaks down. And you start seeing changes that make no sense whatsoever. 

And my risk management system is, and I believe this is true with George although we never talked about it: If I own, let's say, in today's world, the last 10 years at least, if you own stocks and you're short bonds, that most of those 10 years has been the same bet. And if you're long the Euro, that's probably a long risk bet. And you just kind of get a feel in your head of where your matrix is. And I can go in the gym and watch CNBC at 11 o'clock, and I have probably, if you include the whole firm, hundreds of positions on, and all I see on that stupid little ticker is what the S&P is doing, and I can probably tell you our PnL within $2mn. Just because my head knows what my Pound or my Euro position will be doing, and my gold position, based on that. 

And so I sort of have this internal thing where I'm watching everything. But the reason I love the human side as opposed to the quantitative side is there's nothing like my PnL--and you will pick up, Oh, C is not acting the way it was with A the last eight years, and there's something funny. And then you'll start seeing more funniness going on. And I have always thought that if my PnL acts--if things went well that day, and I'm losing money, and I examine what went on, and if that continues, something is really starting to go haywire in the system. 

So my risk management system has always been what I've described, that knowledge, and then my gut, and watching my daily PnL. And if the daily PnL starts acting in a way it shouldn't, instead of going to some quantitative VAR or beta model, go, Oh, I'm okay, the model says I'm okay. 

To me, these models are not only okay, they can get you in huge trouble by causing you a false sense of security when things start going awry, because the model will tell you you're okay, and you will see things happen you've never seen before, whereas if you are a intuitive human trader, you should be able to use your instinct to just start cutting when things aren't acting right."

--

quotedTweet.text:
druck masterclass part 3 - five quotes - invtw w/ Nicolai Tangen (2024) - ht @kevg1412 

invest then investigate + taking L's with confidence + "play from 3rd to 6th inning"

1. invest then investigate - you have 2-3 months

Yeah. Soros used to call it Invest and then investigate. I think I just gave a classic example. I didn't know that much about Nvidia. I just knew that AI--and I had some people here tell me how to play it. So we bought Nvidia, and then we were in the process of doing a lot more work, and then ChatGPT happened. But I've always had the view that markets are smart, they're fast, and they're getting much more so with all the communication and the technology we have today, and that if I hear a concept and I like it, if I wait and spend two or three months analyzing it, I may miss a big part of the move and then psychologically be paralyzed. It's hard to buy a stock you're looking at at 100--it's 160--even if it's going to 400, somehow your head is screwed up and you're waiting for the pullback. So we will buy something, a meaningful position, but not earth shaking, and then really do the work. And if I think we made a mistake, I'll sell it. 

2. cyclicals - look forward 18-24 mo

Stan Druckenmiller: Yes. When I started in the business, I got promoted too early. So before I had really learned the nuts and bolts of the analysis to the extent that I should have, I was promoted to a leadership position, and I had to rely a lot on charts, and I had to rely a lot on intuition. But I found it's not that hard. If you're dealing with a cyclical company and they're losing money, or they're not profitable, and everybody in their industry is shutting capacity down, it doesn't take a rocket scientist to try and envision 18-24 months out, if nobody's adding capacity, they may not be losing money anymore. They might be making a lot of money. 

I have found it's very important never to invest in the present. Always try and envision the situation as you see it in 18-24 months, and then see--if you feel things will be differently than they are now, would security prices reflect that? 

I think that's probably the biggest mistake investors make--is they invest in the present rather than forward looking and looking where the puck is going instead of where the puck is.

3. taking L's with confidence

Nicolai Tangen: But you are quick at selling your losers. What's the key to that?

Stan Druckenmiller: If the reason I bought a stock is no longer the case, I don't care what I paid for it. And if I bought it at 60 and it's 50 because the markets discovered the problem before me, I have I have no emotion whatsoever. Soros was the same way. I didn't really learn it from him, but it was certainly reinforced.

After a while, Nikolai, you also develop enough confidence that you're not afraid to clean the slate and start over because you have the confidence that you'll be successful again and you're not going to sit there in a lazy position that you're not that sure about anymore. 

Just clean house. And if you've been doing it for decades, and it's worked, you kind of have the confidence to take a loss and not worry about it too much. Once I'm out, I'm out.

4. why charts work

Stan Druckenmiller: What I mean by that is, I think one of the reasons charts work, we have--the reason there's support and there's resistance is the resistance is a bunch of people that bought it at 60 and it went down and they've been waiting for three or four years for it to get back to 60 while they could have been in something else that was going up the whole time. 

I just don't care what I paid for a stock. It's absolutely irrelevant in terms of my investment process going forward.

5. soros "will play from the 3rd to 6th inning"

But the point was, with Soros, if he really believes something, the position could never be big enough, particularly if it's in a liquid market. And I learned from him--I like to play the turn, maybe my ego--in a big turn in something. He was perfectly happy to play from the third to the sixth inning. If we go back to baseball terms, if it's a nine inning game, he was perfectly happy to play the third to sixth inning when there was more certainty on much greater leverage. He had more courage than I did in terms of sizing positions. 

I don't think it totally rubbed off on me, but it certainly helped, and it was a huge learning experience. 

I think the major thing I learned with him is it's not whether you're right or wrong, it's how much you make when you're right and how much you lose when you're wrong. And that's what he was--probably as good as anybody who's ever been at.

--

Q: Ordinarily, people think of money managers as having a combination of imagination and analytical ability. If you broke down all the skills into just those two categories, which one would be your particular strength-imagination or analytical ability? 

A: I think my analytical abilities are rather deficient, but I do have a very strong critical faculty. I am not a professional security analyst. I would rather call myself an insecurity analyst. 

Q: That's a provocative statement. What do you mean by that? 

A: I recognize that I may be wrong. This makes me insecure. My sense of insecurity keeps me alert, always ready to correct my errors. I do this on two levels. On the abstract level, I have turned the belief in my own fallibility into the cornerstone of an elaborate philosophy. On a personal level, I am a very critical person who looks for defects in myself as well as in others. But, being so critical, I am also quite forgiving. I couldn't recognize my mistakes if I couldn't forgive myself. To others, being wrong is a source of shame; to me, recognizing my mistakes is a source of pride. Once we realize that imperfect understanding is the human condition, there is no shame in being wrong, only in failing to correct our mistakes.

on "the wilderness years" / the Badlands / re: "idk what to do with my life"

1/3

in a lot of bios, whether it be teddy roosevelt or churchill, u always see a period of 6 months to 2-3 years where they're sort of just off on their own

like TR, after losing his wife and mother in the same day, just bounces to the Badlands and spends a few years kicking it out west with cowboys and shedding the privileged-ness of his upbringing

he credits that to his becoming president, his ability to connect with the common man, and to earn respect independent of the harvard/porcellian image (which can be more of a negative than positive)

2/3

for someone in their early 20's / on the come-up, most advice is pretty straightfoward, at least in the NYC realm...like go do banking, get some pedigree, or go work at Google, just serve a few years in the corporatocracy whether u want to or not, it matters

but sometimes I get DMs from guys in 30s or 40s like, I did that, now I don't know what to do

my reply is always: u are exactly where u should be.

the idea that everything is up and to the right forever, becomes exposed as a fallacy pretty fast...usually around 35-40 there is an "up and out" in most industries

i.e. u become a MD/partner and lock in until age 60, or u go off solo, or u dont make the cut, or u say "fuck this shit"

all lead to, what do I do next

3/3

I prob need to do an article on this w/ a lot more case studies re: "wilderness years" but it almost seems like an imperative or a prerequisite for reaching ones potential, that u sort of just bounce for 6+ months and figure urself out

this means being willing to come back as someone different, which makes ppl uncomfortable

it also means that ur current social circles, u may realize they're not right for u...outgrowing old friends...being judged for "going off the path," etc

so people get stuck between -- do I stay miserable where I'm at, or risk the unknown. and for a lot of ppl, inertia wins out and they choose the former

END

ur best guide here is probably 1x1, behind closed doors, with someone u trust who is in their 50s-60s or higher

like, I can identify the dynamic, but someone that age will have firsthand experience + experience of 20 other ppl they've seen, and how this played out

they'll prob tell u the same, not to sweat "idk what I'm doing" - like, thats the default state lol. a life trajectory is less "up and to the right" than a bowling alley with those bumpers on each side, where u sort of careen back and forth until the lucky few find their mission...and once u do, boom, u ride that until u die.

but if u gotta go into the wilderness, or off to the Badlands to find it...then go to the Badlands.

very solid: "How to Pitch a Stock to a PM, by Bill Miller (Legg Mason)"

(1/2) - INTRO: YOU HAVE 90 SECONDS.

"I want to emphasize in your presentations that if you go into capital markets, you will realize that portfolio managers have ultra-short attention spans.And there is basically no successful portfolio manager of my acquaintance who has ever wanted to hear a story longer than ninety (90) seconds."

"Peter Lynch, when a senior analyst came into a pitch him a stock, would turn on an egg timer for 90 seconds. The analyst had to complete the presentation within 90 seconds and be out of there."

"If you can’t get the portfolio manager’s attention within that time with a convincing case then they will assume that you either don’t have a convincing case or you are not able to articulate it, and you should go back and figure it out."

(2/2) - Stories not Atoms

The world is made of stories, not of atoms. Most people think of the world as analyzing atoms and its constituent parts, and then I am going to figure out how to value it and then describe it. The alternative way to think about it is to construct a convincing story.

Take all your material together and construct a convincing story. If you speak to a portfolio manager, the best thing to say is, “I want to talk to you about Homestore (HOM). It is at $2.25. The 52-week range is $4 to $2 and the all time high was $100 in 2000. 

I think it is a buy for the following five reasons:

1. Bam
2. Bam
3. Bam
4. Bam
5. Bam

The stock is trading a $2 and change. I think it is worth $6 or $8 or whatever. Here is why I think it is worth that. Here are the risks. 

Then you are done. 

In the presentations: no more than five positive points and three negative points. What is it worth and then you are done."

there's an inverse version of this post - "common investing and market maxims that fail to hold."

two that come to mind (and many more will) are "tops are a process, bottoms are an event" and "buy blood in the streets / be greedy when others are fearful"

its not that any of these maxims are outright wrong -- they survive for a reason -- but they are often misapplied or have nuance that needs to be given

the 2nd one is simpler so we'll start there. what happens is that since it came from Buffett, people take it and then just average down over and over in total piece of shit stocks

"buy blood," "greedy when fearful"

the truth is that until u are an advanced-level investor, or at least have several years of experience, u are prob better off being fearful when others are fearful

or at the very minimum, assume that his advice should be applied strictly to the S&P 500

capitalism is vicious and most businesses fail

I don't want to argue back-and-forth on this one but we can agree that 1. its frequently misapplied, and 2. has blown a shitload of accounts...the idea of being contrarian for contrarian sake, or that "down 90%" = "buy"

--

on "tops as a process, bottoms are an event"

this is semi-true

tops are a process but they are literally impossible to forecast/time...ask anyone who has been trading mkts for a long time and they'll agree, NO ONE with real P&L attached ever nails the top...the whole exercise is bigly negative on an expected value basis

peter lynch's "more $ has been lost trying to prepare for recessions, than in recessions themselves" is the best maxim for tops

tops are sneaky as fuck and quite often, even when its obvious shit is bubbly, things progress another 1-3 years...and a lot of times the biggest gains are at the end

so you're trying to dodge down 20%-30%, and miss the up 50-100%.  plus when ppl call "top," they exit and their mind locks them out, they never get back in...hence from the QT "no one is more bearish than a sold out bull."

a fun exercise (one that LLMs can prob help with) - for any top, pull the major news sources (WSJ/BBG etc) and read the daily headlines from top date plus/minus 4 weeks in each direction...get a feel for what the tone and sentiment was, upload to subconscious, may come in handy someday.

then, on bottoms being an event...this is almost never true.

you can have more luck timing bottoms than u can tops, but go study charts urself, u will see its never what people expect

the "event" resembling, a massive capitulation spike low, huge vomit, price-insensitive selling, gigantic volume, etc

these never turn out to be the bottom -- too obvious -- markets are way too cunning.

from a chart standpoint, the SPX in 2008-2009 is what bottoms usually look like (all of this being my humble and frequently-wrong opinion of course) -- I added the chart below

you had the big vomit in oct 2008, the blood in the streets, the "bottoms are an event"

so people bought, you got the oversold bounce, and then from Oct 2008 to March 2009....the SPX went down another 30% or so

more than anything else, bottoms are marked by APATHY.

every bottom I have ever seen or traded, in a stock or an index, it was always apathy bordering on despair or futility

lost track how many times I had this exact exchange on IB with someone:

me: "are you buying"

them: "no, it only goes down" or "no, I bought the spike low then got stopped out 10% lower, fuck this thing...you?"

me: "exact same thought"

and that very day... was always the bottom. seared into my memory each time

so the context/nuance I'd add, is that all the violence means you're probably CLOSE to a bottom...but not only could the bottom be another 30% away, bottoms are not guaranteed to be V-shaped

especially in individual stocks, sometimes a bottom is years long

the stock is bombed out and not going down any further, it ran out of sellers, but that doesnt mean it magically goes up...something has to change the narrative

and you have to factor in trade duration/opportunity cost of capital

it may be "10% down, 50% up," but having $ tied up earning 0% for years isn't a win when the mkt return is 7-8%

so "value is its own catalyst," sometimes true, sometimes not...the duration of the investment affects whether that's wise or not.

--

there's a lot more of these flawed maxims / ones that are hazardous on a standalone basis

but short term, the top maxims in the QT always seem to be the best go-to, almost Occam's razor-y

the big-brain backfitted answers from media and sales/trading desks always are secondary to stuff like:

"why was GOOG down the most yday," bc everyone's long
"why does the tape suck," bc incrementally hawkish fed

there's never an 100% correct answer but the closest thing to it is, fundamentals are always secondary to "max pain to max # of ppl" and "fed policy/liquidity drives everything."

remember, they still don't know what caused the crash of 1987...so, they prob don't know why the nasdaq was off 150 bps yesterday.

no one knows shit

good luck trading

I might have been lucky rather than good, but this single slide from Tarasoff's AMZN deck in 2012, was the core of an entire long pitch

Because you could look at street ests for GAAP EBIT margins 3-5 years out, they were in the 0-4% range

Then, you go back and look at that table and see that in 2004, AMZN had a GAAP EBIT margin of 6.4%

And you're sitting there, like, this has got to be the most obvious pitch I've ever seen, or I'm missing something

"Is there a reason why 6.4% is no longer achievable?"

But if you understood the rev model and fixed cost structure, which prob takes 5-7 years of just looking at businesses...you're like...bro this business is a fucking gigantic warehouse selling shit over the Internet.

There is MASSIVE operating leverage. If revenue was $1B in 2004, and it's $10B in 2014, like, those margins are going to rip. I don't even need to be precise -- if it's above 6.4%, and the street is at 4%, I'm getting paid.

This is actually the type of shit the street will mismodel, and all you had to do was go look at 10-20 years of financials

Obviously you want to spend 2-4 weeks testing EVERY line item in cogs/opex, like, is one of these delevering? Are shipping costs problematic, like, what part of their cost structure is not going to lever on DD%+ rev growth?

And eventually, especially once you layered in the GM% accretive 3P/1P mix shift, you're just like...this is a home run man, the bears think this business is a 0% EBIT margin business and they are about to get their dicks blown off.

In 2014-2015 you had AWS kick in, but this was going to work regardless. You had private label. Then you had advertising. You had all these margin-accretive revenue streams flowing in, and street ests were embarrassingly low.

The bull pitch was making its way around (both from sundheim and tarasoff and many others) but no analyst could get their PM to buy the stock, because the valuation didn't make sense

EBIT margins were 1.8% -- this was trading at 250x EPS and like 100x EBITDA and shit

I vividly remember being like, "on a 6.4% margin, this is cheap as fuck."

"When will they get to 6.4%?" 

"I don't know."

Pitch dead. That's how this went. No one owned it in size until the valuation was "safe" 5 years later, and then all the stock has done is u/p.

So idk what lesson to draw from this one - I think TSLA bulls prob had a similar framework. But between all the tailwinds you had, AND you had bezos who was a ROIC/FCF guy, everything aligned for a massive jockey bet.

I might have been lucky rather than good, but this single slide from Tarasoff's AMZN deck in 2012, was the core of an entire long pitch

Because you could look at street ests for GAAP EBIT margins 3-5 years out, they were in the 0-4% range

Then, you go back and look at that table and see that in 2004, AMZN had a GAAP EBIT margin of 6.4%

And you're sitting there, like, this has got to be the most obvious pitch I've ever seen, or I'm missing something

"Is there a reason why 6.4% is no longer achievable?"

But if you understood the rev model and fixed cost structure, which prob takes 5-7 years of just looking at businesses...you're like...bro this business is a fucking gigantic warehouse selling shit over the Internet.

There is MASSIVE operating leverage. If revenue was $1B in 2004, and it's $10B in 2014, like, those margins are going to rip. I don't even need to be precise -- if it's above 6.4%, and the street is at 4%, I'm getting paid.

This is actually the type of shit the street will mismodel, and all you had to do was go look at 10-20 years of financials

Obviously you want to spend 2-4 weeks testing EVERY line item in cogs/opex, like, is one of these delevering? Are shipping costs problematic, like, what part of their cost structure is not going to lever on DD%+ rev growth?

And eventually, especially once you layered in the GM% accretive 3P/1P mix shift, you're just like...this is a home run man, the bears think this business is a 0% EBIT margin business and they are about to get their dicks blown off.

In 2014-2015 you had AWS kick in, but this was going to work regardless. You had private label. Then you had advertising. You had all these margin-accretive revenue streams flowing in, and street ests were embarrassingly low.

The bull pitch was making its way around (both from sundheim and tarasoff and many others) but no analyst could get their PM to buy the stock, because the valuation didn't make sense

EBIT margins were 1.8% -- this was trading at 250x EPS and like 100x EBITDA and shit

I vividly remember being like, "on a 6.4% margin, this is cheap as fuck."

"When will they get to 6.4%?" 

"I don't know."

Pitch dead. That's how this went. No one owned it in size until the valuation was "safe" 5 years later, and then all the stock has done is u/p.

So idk what lesson to draw from this one - I think TSLA bulls prob had a similar framework. But between all the tailwinds you had, AND you had bezos who was a ROIC/FCF guy, everything aligned for a massive jockey bet.

If you have an alternate take here I'm all ears, otherwise, "that's a 20 hole punchcard...19 to go" is my takeaway.

paragon (cont)

re: random DM q's, just highlighting more shit the pitch does well, starting at top

intro: format

esp "what abt format"

there is no format, anything goes really

fair question if ur young... u want it to look good

but lot of times, its just u and 1-5 people talking, for hours, the "format" isnt a thing except in an intvw

a lot of these VIC pitches are straight text and they're effective

generally though, I think a good north star is: a good pitch should be a LEAN 2 pages and every paragraph punches them in the face - put all the fluffy shit, tables, graphs after that

if u can write 2 pages of straight lasers like this, u can write text

but for 99% of analysts, this would've taken them 10-20 pages to get their point across (and not been nearly as good)

the only way you can write a "text model" like this is from having spent 500 hours staring at Excel, he clearly knew Noble, knew the assets, had familiarty with all this

note how there's no fat, there's no two-paragraph business description

not even "paragon sells rigs"

in one sentence u get the entire setup and it works

if u can write one sentence that good, then do it

u don't need all the formal "variant view" etc,

he does none of that, but its all included in there

best way to frame it is prob, "I have 7-8 paragraphs to make my point, what do I want to talk about in each one, how do I write this shit so hard and tight that by page 1.5 he's buying puts on his phone"

1. maint/growth capex, there's just no other way to have that level of conviction than 5-10+ years doing primary research on the subsector.

and not just developing variant view on maint/growth split, but "here's why mgmt's guide is wrong"

not important where he worked at the time other than, top-tier SM, europe based -- but thats rsch driven by both corp access + primary rsch

so if ur 20 years old u are not gonna write a pitch like this

tricky thing w/ maint/growth capex is u never know when you'll get paid, or if its priced...it affects FCF, but there's no catalyst that shifts mkt perception

esp bc maint capex isnt always disclosed

and then the pitch relies heavily on mgmt being idiots, which can go other way esp on short pitches (very easy to get hyperbolic), but I have no criticism here

but I wouldn't put like "they sounded dumb last transcript" as core of the pitch...its pretty clear that here, he just knows the whole space and how paragon sounds relative to rest (overly optimistic, poor operators)

so on maint/growth/fcf, how to think abt it re: event path, I don't know

but a pitch that goes right into fcf is never wrong, the guy that is fucking around with ebitda multiples is the one who is wrong

this is a far superior analyst to me, and prob 99% of people I've ever met, I blindly defer to him

you know what an ebitda based pitch doesn't take into account?

maint/growth capex

some dumbass prob was flexing 3x, 4x, 5x ebitda on this enterprise (bull or bear)

zero variant view

thats "average" analyst, this is a great analyst

2. all throughout the pitch just running down the ebitda to fcf math as variables

ebitda less capex less cash int less cash taxes gets u fcf

can default to that always, it works, its fundamentally sound, and u avoid messy/immaterial CFO stuff

cash int and cash tax wont change, u are just flexing ebitda and capex

and so as u analyze or adjust line items (revs, cogs, opex) ur right there

3. the rev components, most will go over the head of anyone who doesnt cover the space, but u can see rev = dayrates * utilization

its hard from the outside to see what drives his assumptions but idk if it matters

bc all throughout, he comes at ebitda from several angles.

the model might start at ebitda, a lot of models do (built out by segments, segment ebitdas all flow to main tab ebitda, and u flow down to EPS from there + use the same capex/cash int/cash tax as before, bang, FCF

when you know a company cold, that's what a 10+ year exp L/S analyst buyside model looks like

there's 3-4 variables that matter (as in this pitch) - the BS/CF, whatever

here, it prob goes to ebitda and then the rev math is a sanity check, with individual rigs broken out as a 2nd sanity check above revs

i've seen these models, they are a mess, u model all these individual rigs

but trying to flow 40 rigs into total rev is silly -- and all the warm/cold stacking, u model that, its GIGO

so something like this, esp where u are playing for a terminal outcome...

"better vaguely right than precisely wrong"

the way hes does it is great in the sense of, we have certainty in capex int and taxes to the point where ebitda being 400, 500, 600 or 800...u have a lot of room to be wrong

just constantly running bull/base/bear on everything as u go through it, and u dont even need to be laying it out fancy model style

here's base, if we sensitize x y we get z, other way we get zz

that's how you turn 1 page of text into 1 paragraph

10 page pitch should be 10 paragraphs, cut two, you have a lean 2 pager

4.  fcf

the fcf/dcf math is simple here and unfortunately not every stock is so easy to run in ur head

in any case here u only have a few years fcf remaining so u can sensitize it the way he does

i'm not sure i've seen a pitch on a stable company that could do a "paper dcf" I guess you could call it...if fcfs are predictable then you probably could

mkts price off fcf, not eps

its called conviction, and an appetite for risk

they go hand in hand

there are so few analysts who even have the balls to write a pitch like this, much less get it right

like u better nail this fucking call, because u are straddling the line on cocky vs confident

pitching a fucking equity short with such conviction that at the end, u sprinkle in that this equity is so fucked u can short the bonds

bygone era, u cant do that at a multi

and you'd have to own something against this squiggly little levered equity turd

btw, if u look at the stock chart, I think this IPO'ed at $18 and went to $9

down 50% in a straight line

end

hero shit

courage and conviction are what separate an elite analyst like this from the rest, every PM will smile on these traits bc no one has them

tweets.text:
very solid: "How to Pitch a Stock to a PM, by Bill Miller (Legg Mason)"

(1/2) - INTRO: YOU HAVE 90 SECONDS.

"I want to emphasize in your presentations that if you go into capital markets, you will realize that portfolio managers have ultra-short attention spans.And there is basically no successful portfolio manager of my acquaintance who has ever wanted to hear a story longer than ninety (90) seconds."

"Peter Lynch, when a senior analyst came into a pitch him a stock, would turn on an egg timer for 90 seconds. The analyst had to complete the presentation within 90 seconds and be out of there."

"If you can’t get the portfolio manager’s attention within that time with a convincing case then they will assume that you either don’t have a convincing case or you are not able to articulate it, and you should go back and figure it out."

(2/2) - Stories not Atoms

The world is made of stories, not of atoms. Most people think of the world as analyzing atoms and its constituent parts, and then I am going to figure out how to value it and then describe it. The alternative way to think about it is to construct a convincing story.

Take all your material together and construct a convincing story. If you speak to a portfolio manager, the best thing to say is, “I want to talk to you about Homestore (HOM). It is at $2.25. The 52-week range is $4 to $2 and the all time high was $100 in 2000. 

I think it is a buy for the following five reasons:

1. Bam
2. Bam
3. Bam
4. Bam
5. Bam

The stock is trading a $2 and change. I think it is worth $6 or $8 or whatever. Here is why I think it is worth that. Here are the risks. 

Then you are done. 

In the presentations: no more than five positive points and three negative points. What is it worth and then you are done."

tweets.text:
Basic 2-page stock memo template for ppl to use -- this is version 3.0 or 4.0 since the first one in Summer 2025

Note: this is 100% art, no science. My opinion is just one of many. I will link to the Paragon short pitch though below as I think it's a good "aspirational" 2 pager.

(1/3)

Here is what I think is a clean format.

PAGE ONE:
 
--summary dash (takes up first 50% of page.
--investment thesis in 3-5 bulletpoints
--event path, exit px target, valuation, r/r, base/bull/bear.

You can see below that fit should fit CLEANLY and not look cramped. Majority numbers. Very little words.

To me thats a great flow for page one. All the #'s are in the dash, then "here's the setup" and here's the path to getting paid over next 1-8 quarters.

Don't copy my text too precisely, I bet there's typos, its gobbledygook - its just there as a very loose guide for what you want to be talking about.

So right there, PAGE ONE, that's like 90% of a pitch. Before the mf turns to page two, he's gonna be interested, or he's gonna say "this shit sucks."

It should make clear: Here's the stock today, based on P/E * EPS. Here's where I see EPS for FY2, and here's where I see P/E going as my above FY2 EPS becomes consensus. Price target upside 30% base, then some quick bull/bear flexing for r/r.

PAGE TWO:

I left this wide open for the most part. Chances are, you wrote 10-15 pages on this shit. This page two should be where you take the BEST OF THE BEST, from those 15 pages, and cram it into one page.

I gave ideas, but there is no right or wrong.

Remember: In the Paragon pitch, there is no headers, nothing. He just came with 4 paragraphs of text on page 1, 4 paragraphs of text on page two, and bang, that shit was a wrap.

So, I'm posting this because people send me a lot of really badly formatted pitches, just 8 pages of straight text. 

I am a nice guy, generally. But I have met 200-300 "Dickhead PM's." I am fluent in Dickhead PM voice. I know exactly where in your pitch the DPM will say "LOL this is trash, get the fuck out of my office." 

So your pages 1-2 need to be absolute lightning. That's what I'm trying to emphasize. Pages 3 to 30 will be in the shredder if pages 1-2 suck.

But some mix of these (esp page 2), should be enough to make the pitch. Remember, a pitch is a 90-120 second exercise. If you can't get it done in that time, if they aren't interetsed in 90 secs, your pitch is trash or its too verbose. So keep shrinking it.

I will post links to Paragon below just so you can see that "2 pages is too small wahhh" - no, its not, that motherfucker did in 2 pages what wouldve taken you 20. So its possible.

Going forward, I am just going to reply to most DM's with this post, and say "dude, you gotta condense it more -- too many words -- not enough numbers." Because the Dickhead PM is not gonna make it to page 3 if pages 1-2 are trash.

If I sound like a hardass, well, its better that you get dunked on by some random internet loser, than face-to-face for a pod seat that would change your life.

HTH, and again, if anyone else (professional) has a better format, please post your 2-pagers directly below this. I am not an authroity and I am constantly tweaking these formats because I've found them using them in private/SMB/operating roles as well. So its a lifelong exercise.

END

Good luck pitching,
GB

"TRADE QUIETLY" - on groupthink, copy-trading, pre-mortems, social proof, and borrowed conviction

(1/8)

this is something that affects new/mid-level traders, although the truth is that it affects people all the way at the top when u make ur ideas public

the way I'd frame it is that you want your ideas driven 100% by fundamentals, or making the technically-correct play (ie blackjack), or executing on whatever gameplan you laid out in advance.

thats solely you vs yourself, or you vs the market.

obviously the first "checkpoint" here is, "am I even laying out a gameplan in advance and then executing on it, or am I always just shooting from the hip?"

(2/8)

a gameplan includes a pre-mortem

>what does it look like when I'm wrong?
>where is my stop, where is my exit?
>what are my known unknowns, and unknown unknowns?

that third one to me, is that for any idea, there should be an X that is foreseeable -- "if X happens, I am wrong, and I exit." basically what breaks ur thesis.

additionally, there are also many Y's, unknown unknowns...this is when something comes out of left field, but you recognize it for what it is: "oh shit, my idea is totally fucking wrecked." and you exit.

the 2nd one is where confirmation bias is a killer

(3/8)

this is why I have to at least caution against groupthink/social/community trading

theres always tons of these in crypto, or gme, amc, bored apes, nft's, opendoor, spacemobile, 1000 others like this...I'm not knocking any of these ideas individually, they may work

its more about being brutally honest with urself, because each element of social proof u introduce into a thesis....is taking u further and further away from that 100% pure fundamental/execution standpoint.

groups form groupthink, and groupthink has a nasty way of magnifying confirmation bias

so when X or Y hits -- the risks -- groups tend to coalesce around some way to nullify the truth

"no, this isnt bad" "its actually bullish" etc

(4/8)

this is how you end up with truly massive losses, or ride something to 0

because you have no exit, there is no gameplan, and the market is too powerful for "we all buy together and itll go higher" to be a sustainable investment philosophy

there's some part of human nature where it feels better to ride something to 0, as part of a group, than break off alone and be like "nah this shit is broken, I'm out"

so idk who this is aimed at, I think ppl with 0-2 years experience will be like "lol stfu nerd", its 2-5 who recognize, yeah, I've taken way too many losses doing this

(5/8)

at the highest level, u see this all the time in stuff like VRX, and these are people who genuinely do their homework

but "all the smartest guys I know are also long" has a way of enforcing confirmation bias...making it harder to peel out when u sense something is wrong

and then, right now, lets say you are gigalong semis and very very public about it

tomorrow, lets say out of left field, SemiCo announces "we just brought 50% new supply online overnight...capacity expansion"

this affects the entire industry/pricing superstructure -- revs, GM%, EPS, all those ests have to come down to reflect new supply

(6/8)

so even though your public-gigalong-stance may not be "broken," u could run thru all ur models and suddenly the risk/reward isnt there anymore.

the mkt priced in this new information and now all ur ideas are 50% down, 50% up, totally balanced

meanwhile u are super public on this thesis

very very few people have the brutal self-efficacy, honesty w self, immunity to social proof, sharp intellect, whatever u wanna call it....to just come out the next day like "yea thats a wrap, we exited"

confirmation bias is incredibly powerful, u have to treat all social/non-fundamental tentacles as poisonous, toxic, negatives that take u farther away from pure fundamental execution (which is hard enough on its own).

(7/8)

on borrowed conviction...very old wisdom to never trade on someone else's tips

but twtr/social media have exacerbated this to an entirely new level

here is the issue. someone says they like X, u buy it

but now, every time news comes out and the stock moves 10-20%, u are looking to that person for what to do next

this is not sustainable, at all...bc keep in mind, they're victim to all the biases we just laid out

so they may make the technically-incorrect play, because they've put so many ppl in it, that social proof kicks in.

(8/8)

I have learned this the hard way many times, I used to email out ideas to groups, and only in the rearview can I look back and recognize "I stayed in these positions longer than I should have, neg P&L came from social proof, confirmation bias blinded me to broken thesis" etc

conviction can never be borrowed. if someone else has an idea u like, thats fine, but u have to write ur own gameplan

start to finish...pre mortem, what it looks like when wrong, how u would navigate all the various newsflow items that would come out

u never ever want to be in a position of looking to some other guy for "what do I do now," also because u never learn anything when ur wrong, u just blame them

whereas sourcing ur own ideas, going thru the entire lifecycle of the trade start-to-finish...when it goes wrong, u can reflect and then iterate on where u fucked up.

END

this is a deep and complex topic but I think I've hit most of the basics...munger's "psychology of human misjudgment" is all about stuff like this

I pulled this below, hit LLM's with this stuff until u understand it

ultimately u have to do ur own due diligence always, think for urself, conviction can never be borrowed

dont share ur ideas, dont talk ideas, dont use other people's ideas...only takes u farther from reality.

random but if ur in a drawdown rn, say 25-50%, which I sense many are because everyone is in the same trades

“When you’re in a hole, stop digging”

It tends to be a net benefit to eat a bunch of losses, clean up the P&L screen, and refresh ur mind. Unrealized P&L clogs the brain, always

Rethink all the losing positions that u exited, start from stage zero 

There is nothing stopping u from putting the same trade right back on if u decide its best - there’s wash sales to account for, that’s it

But u cannot underestimate mental capital, and the simple “clear the decks” of having an emptier book + capital to deploy

Turns u opportunistic again vs defensive and anxious 

“You don’t have to make it back the way you lost it”

The biggest risk is that many inexperienced ppl go on tilt when they’re down say 50%, “I’m already so fucked”

Blowing out of losses puts in the bottom for ur near term P&L. It’s always more refreshing than it is negative 

The other mental pitfall is ppl assuming that the stock has to go here or there, or back where it came from

Brotha - it doesn’t have to do ANYTHING. The current price is the price. Nothing is guaranteed beyond that

And so again, eating L’s cuts off all those wirings in your brain, refreshes anchoring and cost basis. No more “should”

Next, u have ppl saying “what if I miss the rebound”

Bro if u are trading on that short a time frame, 1-2 weeks, even less than 1 month, u just aren’t approaching this thoughtfully…very herky jerky, day to day, driven by FOMO and non fundamental factors

You must eliminate “what if I miss a 2 week rally right after I sell it” from your brain

This is pure bad. All bad. Will only lead u astray. 

Until you’re comfortable just chilling and watching, and watching a stock rally after u sell it without freaking or chasing…ur emotions aren’t where they need to be. 

You visualize, u say “I am taking the L, I am ready for it to go up 30% right after I click sell, and that’s just fuckin life. There’s 100000 other stocks. I’ll find another”

Could write endlessly on this but being in a big draw over a weekend, v easy to be fucked mentally, sweating futures open, like you are driven by fear and emotion and HOPE. None of which are viable 

Your best bet is to blow the fuck out of anything down big causing u agita. You can buy it back higher in a month if it was a bad sale. But think process not outcome. Also given that ur trading like shit, taking a week off to heal the mind, keeping core longs on, is only gonna help u

Brings u back with fresh eyes

So Mon ideally, u go from 100% invested and in 50% drawdown, to just being mostly cash. Start from scratch. Ur capital base is ur capital base, the stock prices are the stock prices. History is HISTORY - it’s IRRELEVANT. 

Protect ur mental capital

I’ve made every mistake and watched 500 ppl make the same ones so I tend to know the ruts where ppl are at…I feel it from DM’s

Down 30-50%, like, fuck, I liked this idea but I’m smoked and the tape sucks

Take the L, accept that u may miss a sharp rebound, LIVE WITH IT. 

There is a hard ceiling for any trader who cannot take L’s with equanimity

You will never progress until u are cool as a fan with lock-in of losses, mental refresh, stabilize, then go on attack.

U can attack in an entirely new sector or name, like swap into what’s printing ATH’s, stop fighting secular bear overhangs, and chances are u do not belong in semis

Rethink it all

“Stop doing what isn’t working”

Mental capital is everything. Stay liquid and nimble and opportunistic. Deep red unrealized losses are poisonous roots that disrupt clear thinking

Cut those motherfuckers on sight. All temporary. All can be re entered later. 

Protect ur mental kiddo. Good luck trading

Druck masterclass part two -- 8 parts -- risk, concentration, tape feel -- from 2022 intvw with John Collison (ht @kevg1412)

1. inside of the stock market as forecaster -- micro as macro

Yeah, one of the ironies of my style, maybe it's because I was a dropout of a Ph. D. program in economics at University of Michigan, is that I don't use what traditional economists use to predict the economy, which is things like employment, and a bunch of macro top down statistics. In fact, I started my career as a bank and chemical analyst. 

And over time, I learned that the inside of the stock market had a very, very prescient message about future economic activity. And for whatever reason, stocks tend to lead the fundamentals by somewhere between 6 and 12 months. 

And you can even go beyond that and look at industries that lead the economy and industries that lag the economy. The obvious one that everyone knows about is housing, has traditionally been looked at as a leading industry. Retail has a slightly capital goods lag. And what we've done historically, is actually, even though you refer to me as a macro investor, and many people have, is we do the macro by a compilation of listening to companies and doing a bottoms up analysis of industries that lead the economy and industries that lag the economy. 

And if the leading industries are turning up or turning down, that's a signal. And that's worked beautifully historically.

2. (cont macro/micro)

What was going on is, central banks were buying trillions of dollars and manipulating the price of bonds. So there was no signal. I don't think you get that tainting if you look inside the stock market. You could get it in the stock market as a whole. 

But if you do this approach, where you look at industries and which lead, which lag, and you put the puzzle together, it's been prescient over time, and it's certainly allowed us to consistently, the last 20 or 30 years, outperform the Fed in terms of economic forecasts.

3. invest first, investigate later -- you have 2-3 weeks

Well, you mentioned earlier that the business has gotten a lot more competitive than it was 20 or 30 years ago. There is so much information out there, and so many smart people in our industry have come in since 2000, when the financial renumeration went crazy, that you just don't have the time you had when I got in the business. 

When you hear a good idea, if you wait two or three weeks, a lot of times now, believe it or not, 60 or 70% of the move will have taken place.

4. shit moves fast -- 2-3 weeks, again

Yeah. And when you enter it, there's no story out there. So hopefully, in 10 days, if you're wrong, there's still no story. There's not going to be some bear story because the guy's giving you a bull story. 

But if there is a bull story, it's quite likely that somebody else is gonna discover it over the next two or three weeks. These analysts go out to dinner with each other like four nights a week and try out their ideas. 

And a lot of times they don't wait for the portfolio manager because they're trying to make themselves look good with the other guys at dinner, too. I used to do that when I had more energy.

5. idea velocity + how stale ideas lead to drawdowns

Yeah, it's, it's completely contrary to what they teach in business school, which is, if you're highly diversified, you have less risk than if you're highly concentrated. I don't believe that at all. As an investor, when I think most people get into much trouble is when they have stale longs or stale shorts. 

When you've got 15, 20% of your asset base, or some of the time in macro positions, I'll have 200-300%. Believe me, they're not getting stale. And you have to have ruthless discipline, and you're coming in every day. 

Just, to quote Andy Grove, you could not be more paranoid. And you're constantly reevaluating. And I think it leads to an open mind. So yeah, I would also say, people ask me what I learned from George Soros. I thought, when I went there, I was gonna learn what made the Yen and the Deutsche Mark go up and down, and that kind of thing. 

6. SIZING WINNERS

No, what I learned was, sizing is probably 70 or 80% of the equation. It's not whether you're right or wrong, it's how much you make when you're right, and how much you lose when you're wrong. I've also found, as an investor, I believe in streaks. You see it in baseball, you see and everything else. I see it in investing. Sometimes you're seeing the ball, sometimes you're not. One of my number one jobs, is to know whether I'm hot or cold. And when I'm hot, I'm supposed to turn the dial way up. Not say, okay, I'm a 40% this year, let's go, this will look good at the end a year ago, take a break. 

No, you got to make hay while you're hot. And then when you're cold, the last thing you should do is try and make big bets to get back to even. You should tone yourself down. So believe it or not, that's part of the all your eggs in one basket. Not only do I have to see the investment that really excites me, I also have to see myself sort of being in a good trading rhythm.

7. i'm actually lazy but I have passion.

I think it's very relevant. I was pretty lazy in college. And I never considered myself a particularly hard worker. But I'm so passionate about our business, that it's almost like a compulsive gambler that has a way to channel his compulse. And the fact that every event in the world affects some security price somewhere, and the fact that I'm so intellectually stimulated trying to imagine the world 12 to 18 months from now, versus the way it looks in the present, and security prices, how they would reflect that. I just find it so stimulating, it makes everybody think I'm a hard worker, because I'm attracted to the game. 

So in this game, I am a hard worker. But I actually think there's a life lesson there. I've seen young people who, when they find their passion, who had kind of looked like they were lazy, or lost their way or weren't very driven, become very driven. I just happen to be passionate about this particular discipline. So I don't know whether I have a word hard work ethic, but that's the end result of my passion.

8. advice to young ppl

Well, the first thing I tell them is, if you're not really passionate, if you don't love this stuff, go do something else. And I've hired guys with IQs 50 or 60 points higher than me who stink in my business, because...and by the way, they could be off inventing or starting new companies that could do very well. 

But I actually think the next 4-5 years are going to be tailored to the skill set that worked for me in the 80s and 90s, which was all sorts of macro chaos, and I would encourage them to learn all the asset categories and how they integrate. Not easy. If I was a tech investor, I would certainly be learning...we had the internet wave, we had the cloud wave, cloud doesn't look like it's over yet. But I would certainly be looking into blockchain very deeply, into the possible disruption it might take. But I think fundamentals are fundamentals. Look, when companies are losing money, capacity is always going to shrink and their margins are gonna look better in three years. When companies are over earning, their margins are going to come down in three years. I think all that stuff will be out there. 

I think the great thing about my original mentor, Spiros Drelles in Pittsburgh, was he made me focus on what moves the stock price. Like you can't just say, Stan, okay, this is a great company, and the earnings are great. He said, tell me how people are going to think differently in 18 or 24 months about the situation than they're thinking now. 

That would be my number one advice to the young people. Do not, do not invest in the present. The present is not what moves stock prices. Change moves them. And I want you to try and envision a different world in a year and a half from now and where these security prices would trade versus now, given the world you envision. That would be my number one advice to a young person getting into the business.

--

Writing = "a vivid and continuous fictional dream."

this is another serious book -- John Gardner really is the "axe" -- but one which can be enjoyed as a reader of novels/fiction, anyone who appreciates art, or the craft, or is a student of the game, or who just wants to know more about what makes great writing great

that term ("vivid and continuous dream") is all I want to highlight in this post, I won't summarize the whole book, nor could I tbh, as half of it went over my head

Gardner will just casually pick apart in random paragraphs the faults of a Faulkner or Hemingway, and not as some loser critic, but just as someone with a master eye for the craft... he senses details that you or I wouldn't catch in 1000 years

but thinking of a great piece of writing as "a vivid dream" is such an astute term...novel readers want to be so caught up in the "dream" that they forget they're even reading.

and so good reading and good writing, are both a function of remaining that the vivid and continuous dream remains unbroken...which is prob why encountering an LLM generated sentence feels mentally like crashing into a 80-car pileup

I pulled together 10 quotes from him, from reviewers, and from around the internet to drill this point home:

--

1. “All good books are alike in that they are truer than if they had really happened and after you are finished reading one you will feel that all that happened to you and afterwards it belongs to you; the good and the bad, the ecstasy, the remorse and sorrow, the people and the places and how the weather was.”

2. ...By continuous, he means nothing on the page distracts the reader from the story, nothing makes him backtrack, nothing makes him have to pause and think -- he may pause and think because something stirs his imagination, but we don't want him to pause because he has to figure something out to understand the story.

3. "Writer and teacher John Gardner had a concept he called the fictional dream, which was the idea that fiction does its job by creating a dream state for the reader, and as long as the writer is doing a good job of maintaining that dream state, the reader won't "wake up" from it and will continue to read and believe in the fictional world the writer has created. 

4. Gardner argues that this fictional dream first happens in the writer's head, and the writer's job is to write it down for the reader...Gardner's central argument holds that effective fiction must create a "vivid and continuous dream" in the reader's mind, an immersive experience that engages the reader emotionally and intellectually as if the events were real. This requires the writer to uphold moral and aesthetic seriousness, treating fiction as a rigorous art form committed to truth, precise detail, and human values rather than mere entertainment or self-expression."

5. Central to his framework is the notion that great fiction creates a "vivid and continuous fictional dream" in which the reader experiences the narrative world as immediate and real, engaging the senses and emotions in a manner akin to lived experience.

6. Gardner describes this dream as arising when the writer presents dramatized actions through concrete, sensory images rather than abstract exposition, allowing readers to perceive settings, characters, and events with full conviction: "the writer sets up a dramatized action in which we are given the signals that make us 'see' the setting, characters and events... so that we seem to move among the characters, lean with them against the fictional walls, taste the fictional gazpacho, smell the fictional hyacinths."

7. He stresses that anything interrupting this immersion—such as technical errors, authorial intrusions, or deliberate reminders of the text's constructed nature—snaps the reader out of the experience, rendering the fiction unsatisfying. Great fiction, in contrast, sustains the illusion so powerfully that emotional responses mirror those in real life: "Great fiction can make us laugh or cry, in much the way that life can... Somehow the fictional dream persuades us that it’s a clear, sharp, edited version of the dream all around us."

8. Gardner "...emphasizes the creation of a "vivid and continuous fictional dream" for the reader, treating any disruption—whether from clumsy prose or emotional inauthenticity—as a serious flaw."

9. Gardner presents the "vivid and continuous dream" as the central metaphor for successful fiction, asserting that good writing must immerse the reader in an uninterrupted, convincing fictional world that feels real and absorbing. The "vivid" element requires precise, concrete details, strong verbs, fresh imagery, and emotional authenticity to generate clear mental pictures and powerful feelings, while the "continuous" aspect depends on flawless execution to prevent any disruption—such as factual errors, inconsistencies, awkward shifts in perspective, or clumsy phrasing—from breaking the reader's immersion. Gardner stresses that any flaw waking the reader from this dream state undermines the fiction, making the creation of this seamless experience the writer's primary obligation.

10. One of the book's most lasting contributions is its popularization of the concept of the "vivid and continuous dream," which holds that successful fiction must create an immersive, uninterrupted experience in the reader's mind, appealing to the senses and sustaining narrative logic without drawing attention to the text itself. This principle has become a central tenet in teaching realist fiction, guiding writers to avoid disruptions such as poor diction or self-conscious language that might jolt the reader from immersion. Gardner's discussions also helped bring terms like "psychic distance"—the varying degrees of emotional and perceptual closeness between narrator and character—and "profluence"—the forward causal momentum that propels a story—into common usage among writers and educators.

--

last, from the writer's perspective:

“In the writing state—the state of inspiration—the fictive dream springs up fully alive: the writer forgets the words he has written on the page and sees, instead, his characters moving around their rooms, hunting through cupboards, glancing irritably through their mail, setting mousetraps, loading pistols. The dream is as alive and compelling as one’s dreams at night, and when the writer writes down on paper what he has imagined, the words, however inadequate, do not distract his mind from the fictive dream but provide him with a fix on it, so that when the dream flags he can reread what he’s written and find the dream starting up again. This and nothing else is the desperately sought and tragically fragile writer’s process: in his imagination, he sees made-up people doing things—sees them clearly—and in the act of wondering what they will do next he sees what they will do next, and all this he writes down in the best, most accurate words he can find, understanding even as he writes that he may have to find better words later, and that a change in the words may mean a sharpening or deepening of the vision, the fictive dream or vision becoming more and more lucid, until reality, by comparison, seems cold, tedious, and dead.”

--

if ur a serious reader of novels both books are worth your time ("art of fiction" first, "becoming a novelist" second)...and it should go without saying that if you have even the faintest interest in writing well, both are a drop-what-you're-doing and buy them immediately.

quotedTweet.text:
really good book on writing, I think one of the canonical texts

even if ur just a reader - "writing makes you a better reader, and reading makes you a better writer" - this book fits that

(1/4)

"There are only two plots in literature: a hero goes on a journey, or a stranger comes to town." -- that quote gets attributed to Gardner and is why I bought the book

turns out its apocryphal. but theres a lot in here thats just as valuable, and its easily something he could have said

its very clear this man is a master and is fluent not just in the craft but the way he dissects everyone from Faulkner to Dostoevsky, in language that did not occur to u naturally

this is not a "difficult" book re: length or language used. however, its very challenging in that a single sentence will make you stop and reflect on how applicable it is to you. you get out of it what you put into it

(2/4)

people see "creative writing" and think, I dont write, I dont need that. this is wrong

much of creative writing/fiction is simply your ability to describe day-to-day life or human nature

examples
-describe the face of the woman you love
-describe the way your friend walks
-an old hemingway one: watch people getting out of taxis and describe how they differ

etc...once u try this, and put words on paper, u will realize that ur writing is horrible, nondescript or cliche

then u will look at ur bookshelf and say "I need to see how the old masters did this"

then u realize u never really "read" these books.

this is how writing makes u a better reader.

(3/4)

whether an ability to describe everyday life is important to u or not...idk

if ur wired like me, as soon as a weakness of yours is brought to ur attention, u will not rest until its removed or progress is made

if ur reading this u prob come from a business background where u are instructed, more or less, to "tell, dont show"

this is the opposite of writing about life, where the cardinal rule is 

"Show, don't tell."

so u have to both unlearn some of what u know, plus add an entirely different skillset.

(4/4)

I finished this 3-4 weeks ago and it has been bouncing around in my head since...thats how u know it was good

I never really rec shit that I just finished, bc it takes time to see if the writing had staying power.  the great ones plant themselves in your subconscious

so I would say if you are someone who either appreciates great writing, or wants to improve for their own sake, this should prob be on ur shelf, and is one u will end up reading multiple times.

this is how it should be if u take risk for a living/in a "performance" role where outcomes justify process

have to unwire and rewire a lot of shit, like, it doesnt matter if u only work 1 minute a day, or only make 1 decision per year and not 1000

autopilot all that
