known unknowns, fear, risk, countervailing forces, avoidance of pain, what ppl will think

"how do I know when it's time?" (part 2)

same topic as QT...u have an idea or something u want to do, and u don't know if it's time.

but you are 100% stuck in solo mental warfare.

we are going to nail down as many variables as possible, and make concrete from the intangible

this is how u exit mental warfare mode, or at least create some order from chaos

1. What are the major countervailing forces?

what lurks in the "no" column of your mind?

they tend to be:

- what people will think
- fear
- avoidance of pain

The first one, it can be important, but there are also times where it doesn't matter and you have a false belief system.

If you were to take a risk, random ideas being...build a business, create videos, write a book, do a podcast ....anything where you think, "I risk looking stupid in public."

these are zero downside scenarios when you fail, there is no "what people will think"

you always seem to gain 1000x that in the process.

people aren't thinking about you kid. maybe your content flitters across their feed, maybe they like it, or ignore it, or someone takes 10 seconds to comment "u look like a fgt" and then keeps scrolling

no matter what, you're ancient history within hours

2. 

on starting a business and failing

millions of people have opinions on this

consensus imo: "more upside than downside."

put aside money gained or lost, it matters but it also comes and goes like water, and it ends up being less important for the enjoyment of life than you anticipated.

we covered this in the QT, so we'll keep moving

next is fear

you are afraid of failure. this is natural. but keep in mind everything you've ever read about failure... it's embraced, encouraged, welcomed, and suffering breeds growth.

there's a reason for all this talk, because it's real.

I can't un-fear you, unfortunately, but I can tell you that there is a pretty reliable method for conquering a fear.

you take a deep breath, u grab ur nuts, and u go sprinting at it at full speed. 

duality of life. nothing is ever as good as it seems, but nothing -- including fear -- is ever as bad as it seems.

"fears melt away as they are faced head-on."

3. 

last is avoidance of pain.

This is tricky because to accomplish anything worth accomplishing, you have to leave some possibility open that shit is just going to get fucked up and not work.

You will be in pain, you'll lose relationships, friends, money

everything is risk/reward. this is the risk side of the equation.

I think about this exact topic a lot, because I've gone back and forth over the years between

>100% all-in on one idea
>making smaller bets, planting seeds, buying OTM calls, trying to get as many "small downside + massive upside" situations working for me as possible

I don't know if either is "right," I'm just trying to figure out which is right for me

The former is my default way of operating, "burn the boats" in everything

The latter sounds very intelligent, big-brained, "hard to lose,"

way more prudent than going all-in on urself...diversified, "somethings gotta work," 

blah blah blah...

4.

if I got a stock pitch like that, as a long, I'd say "no fuckin chance it works" 

nothing is that obvious

wow yeah I'd love a portfolio full of "down 0% up 100%'s"

my buddy and I used to call these FLAs🚨

short for "Free Lunch Alert 🚨"

it's down 0%, up 100%? 

guarantee it goes down 75% in a straight line, express, no stops, transfer at jamaica.

but next time someone sends u a garbage pitch u could be real passive aggressive and hit them with the 

"wow FLA🚨"

ADBE at 7x...u don't say

that is a scrumptious free lunch right there u have found, my friend

ty, tyvm...in fact, ty hilton (the summa of ty's)

feels like just last month adbe was 8x, then before that 9x, then 10x

each month a turn of multiple gets lopped off and the free lunch becomes even free'er

what usually happens with these is everything is fine for 4-5 quarters

then they guide EPS 50% below street and the "true" multiple reveals itself not as 8x, but 16x

expensive lunch alert 💰

5.

but on risk/reward, the two scenarios I laid out before -- I sense that God won't let you thread the needle

you can't take no risk, and expect big reward

I'm quietly hoping this happens but deep down I know it's just not the way the world works 

also because putting your ass in the line will motivate you, and that motivation is probably what gets the W in the long run

so, I am not a serial entrepreneur, but my gut says that you can only fuck around for so long with smaller ideas and small dick money and small conviction

it's pretty rare that I know what to do, and choose not to do it

but here I'm once burned, twice shy

I know the correct move is to figure out your best idea and push some fucking chips in

and that it's just mental masturbation, tugging ur worm in the mirror, until u go for it

but u trade markets long enough, u develop scars lol...just a walking encyclopedia of all the L's you've taken.

I'm torn bw "what I know works for me" and "recency bias where it actually didnt work for u"...instinct uber alles.

6.

going back in time...

if I was say 25-35, and trying to map out the future

this is how I would break it down

we talked about the risks of risk, lose $, lose friends, divorce, etc

your comfort with your risk scenario, this downside scenario, is what really dictates everything.

Some people have zero risk appetite, who I have known my whole life...they would just never think this way, they're not wired for it

Others intuitively embrace risk in all things and in all forms.

So if you have been trading markets, now you have risk in the form of "what does my downside in xyz real life scenario look like?" 

it's just a risk.

there's no dollars, but risk is risk.

Is this risk of pain worth the rewards?

Yes, boom, jump off the cliff.

if it works great, if not, I took what felt like a favorable risk/reward proposition.

blackjack mindset....9,999 hands to go.

so there are minds that are constantly viewing everything in risk terms, underwriting risk, and will take pretty much any risk thats heavily skewed in their favor.

what are the risks of writing a book, of sending this tweet, relative to the rewards? favorable, lets go.

8.

If you already think this way, then all near-term opportunities, or any risk/reward proposition, can be framed thru the same lens.

It's never different.

And with each risk you grow incrementally more comfortable with risk.

So I think that's the very best advice I could give in helping someone re-wire their mind for: I am going to take lots of risks in my life but they feel new and different and unusual.

They really aren't. Like, take out a piece of paper, or Excel, and list out all the non-monetary shit you are worried about.

9.

-Money: what's risked, what's lost, what would you be left with

-Family/friends: less of a factor than you think, and often, they are anti-risk because they never want to see you in pain. They will tend to steer you towards "white picket fence, W2, American dream, safe, sound, boring life."

So when you deviate from that path, their reaction doesn't mean a whole lot...

"are you sure," "that sounds risky," "why aren't you doing what everyone else does"

and so on.

They mean well, but just be aware there is a permanent bias and not one that has ever detered someone from following their heart.

And then lay out all the other risks and rewards and variables. 

Just stare at it.  Most of it is hyperventilation or shit you can't control.

My hope is that having it staring back at you from a piece of paper, will solidify it to where u say, "fuck it, I now grasp the known unknowns, let's rip."

10.

It will always come down to:

1. Gameplan
2. Daily execution of gameplan.

So all the "what if this" in a risk scenario, well, you'll get there only if you don't exectute. And if you don't execute, you can't complain.

Is that negative outcome something you'd accept if you can't execute? 

If yes, then go.

You can run this out over 50, 100, 200 ideas, the variables don't change.

END

I would even say taking larger and larger risks is the best way to get comfortable, and what I mean is, if you went on some podcast or something, and you talked for an hour, and it went public...a lot of your fears are going to die.

Because people will talk shit, they'll laugh at you, your respective failures and uglinesses will be mentioned as a human...and then 24 hours later they disappear and move on.

And now you understand risk, reward, failure, and the crowd, so now other risks seem less daunting. But you had to take a different, unrelated risk...and it worked as a mechanism, didn't it?

Behind anything that has ever gotten done, ever, is those same two words.

"fuck it"

No one ever had God come down from the sky and say: "now is the time, here's everything you need."

Everything began with some guy or girl with a loosely-formed plan in their head, who just kind of shrugged 

absolutely no fucking idea if this is a good idea

but

I wanna put the plaza hotel right here

fuck it [plop]

some guy legit said

"I want to start a business called Ollie's Bargain Basement"

followed by "fuck it" followed by 1000 fuckin boxes

no fear

All those Portuguese and Spanish mf's just hopping into boats...let's sail West and we'll see what happens, muchachos.

they came in search of America

and they left with a 36-pack of Dove Mango-Cucumber Exfoliating Face Wash from Ollie's Bargain Basement

24 hours later, the Inquisition began

Oswald Spengler spoke of this

--

u have to always ask: 

"why not me?"

Same question everyone else asked, and they made shit happen.

Final quote on risk, from Larry Hite:

"I have two basic rules about winning in trading as well as in life:
1. If you don't bet, you can't win.
2. If you lose all your chips, you can't bet."

that's a falsehood to be dispelled bc I've gotten tweets like, "oh at 30 this happens, and 35 this happens," I might've said the same younger, idk

but if u do nothing, here's what happens: nothing

all u will do is decay.

2/7

whereas if u are 31 and u just go through it all in a single year, ur mind goes from 31 to 50 (in the best way possible)...experience is what makes someone seasoned and wise to the ways of the world

this dictates how ur friend group revolves, there are ppl who play it safe lifestyle-wise and there are people who take risk

paths diverge, u were on the same highway younger, now u just each took ur off ramp

jung's "1st half/2nd half of life" framework is prob the best

u will have friends who cross the plane (due to pain, experience), whereas others don't....idk if it's your choice

3/7

all the ppl I'm closest friends with, had their lives fall apart at some point in their late 20's or 30's or early 40's

lost all their $, divorce, drugs, lawsuit, jail, business failure

all the same personality type, high energy, high risk appetite...not the type to ever say "x happened to me," not sympathy seekers. just a part of ur nature + usually paired with, "the speed limit was 65, I should've been doing 75-80, I was at 100"

like u were just going at too fast a speed, for too long, where a bad outcome of some sort was due. 

and thats where u finally come face to face with ur own mortality, and thats when u shed the skin of ur 1st half of life and enter the 2nd half of life.

4/7

life goes on. ur new life is totally different from ur old life, but life goes on

and as time goes on, u see lots of other people, normal, quiet, God-fearing...who go thru periods of severe upheaval

they didn't even do anything wrong, like...u just get used to the fact that ur life, or anyone's life, can change, forever, in an single day. 

and the life u knew, is gone.

but out of the ppl I'm close with, every single person, if asked, "would u go back in time if u could and erase the actions + consequences"... says fuck no.

because u see who u are now, vs who u were then, and its like, are u kidding me, that guy wasn't built to be calm in chaos. he thought he was, but he wasn't.

and if u reflect on any of ur own errors or mistakes u will see its the same answer.  

everything u know about markets came from losing $...u cant go back and get the $, without giving up the experience/wisdom.

plus...the way I phrase it is that "fears melt away as they are faced head on."

nothing in life is ever as good as it seems, and nothing is as bad as it seems...pain is intense and short-lasting, and then u recognize the fear was always greater than reality.

and at a certain point u have made every mistake in the book, which has a massive positive impact on ur life

would u advise that someone go thru the consequences to get there...not intentionally. but dont live in fear either

and in this light, u recognize regret as silly and pointless in the self-pity/self-flagellation sense. just do better.

5/7

so that gets to the mcconaughey quote below which doesn't quite track

he says "40's were great but I see my 50's midlife crisis coming"

my buddy was like, "his 50-something, was my 30-something."

and that's what I said in the intro, and I agree

the comments on the 40s are dead on, but they usually come from someone who was just shipwrecked where u change ur life.

and hes setting expectations poorly for the majority of ppl who will inevitably have something turn their life upside down in their 40's, despite dodging the reaper so far.

6/7

once u understand that time ticks in linear fashion, whereas experience/wisdom come in massive chunks -- "weeks where decades happen" -- the way I see it, is that I want my experience to stay 10-30 years ahead of my age

my biggest concern is that I'm not dying enough deaths

you watch a year go by and compare the time elapsed vs the experience gain

and what would be a good year for most ppl, like, pain and failure sort of morph ur tolerance -- all for the better

ur level of risk, and ability to withstand pain, is now so much higher than normal and higher than what urs used to be. 

u notice it as hardship/adversity just sort of bounces off, and other people freak out over things where ur thinking, "u better pray nothing more major than this happens bc u are ill-equipped"

but each day that u do not die new deaths, or risk dying new deaths, whatever that means to u...is another day where the reaper closes the gap.

and ur age catches up to your experience

I don't have a crystal ball but when ur 80, I get the sense these moments and feelings are what u regret, far moreso than any mistakes u made.

the feeling of wasted time is never pleasant, ever

7/7

is this a good framework or one to mull over - unclear and it's out of my control. 

when ur gut, ur spirit talk to u, u listen.

it goes without saying to think for urself, never blindly take advice from any stranger on the internet or walk their path...shit might be fucked up, but work for them, but its not for u.

everything has to be unique to u, I'm merely here waving mirrors and lights around hoping it helps u see urself clearer.

I would frame mine if it resonates, in the healthiest light, as:

"I know where my ceiling is, I am nowhere near it...I'm not growing fast enough, I can handle a lot more discomfort/pain/risk than I am taking right now, and my lifestyle permits it."

and when all these things align, like, u gotta fuckin shoot.

thats what ppl don't get..."all clear" is the green light. 

there is no starting gun, only a window of opportunity, which remains open for God only knows how long.

its only when the light turns red, window slams shut, and and they're stuck, that they look back: "shit...the opening was there for 2 years, I was just being a pussy."

end

this is the answer that anyone will give u, to every and any question beginning with: "how do I know when its time to (take x risk)"

u never do, no one ever has....age old question, one I used to ask, always gonna be met with a shrug.

"motherfucker just went for it"

and thats 100% bw u and the man in the mirror...there's nothing on twitter for ya.

c'est la guerre ⚔️

Robert Caro Q&A...great answer here

Q: "Why should business executives be interested in the life of Lyndon Johnson?"

A: As far as I’m concerned, biography is a tool for understanding power: how it is acquired and how it is used. I never had any interest in writing about a man or woman just to tell the life of a famous person. All my books are about power and about how leaders use power to accomplish things.

We’re all taught the Lord Acton saying that power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. But the more time I spend looking into power, the less I feel that is always true. What I do feel is invariably correct—what power always does—is reveal. Power reveals.

from Napoleon's 1812 retreat from Russia...crazy detail on the human condition

a lot of bios don't go into the Vilnius disaster

after the Berezina, the Grande Armée marched 150 miles in temperatures of minus 35...men just toppling over dead, mid-march, from the extreme cold

Vilnius was supposed to be salvation, a massive supply hub packed with food, shelter, ammo, etc

The city was overwhelmed on arrival but the soldiers mostly were able to get a good meal and a warm night's rest

This is where Napoleon decides to return to Paris to stem rumors of a coup, and having realized the campaign was lost, he abandons the army and puts Murat in charge.

Murat almost immediately loses his nerve, freaks out when some Russian cossacks appear, and orders a premature evacuation of Vilnius the next morning

This is the material on the page...the men were broken, they couldn't move:

--

"When he heard the bugle sound the alarm in the early hours and began rousing his men, many, even veterans of the Egyptian and Italian campaigns, simply refused to budge. “That night of complete rest around a good fire had been enough to extinguish their courage and their energy,” he wrote. “They were overcome by a general drowsiness, a heaviness in the head which seemed to obscure the faculty of thought. Stupefied, and as if drunk, they attempted to get to their feet, only to fall back heavily.” The story was the same in other units.

--

then, Prince Wilhelm describes stopping at Vilnius as an error, as the men would have been better off continuing to march:

--

“Instead of staying a whole day in Vilna, it would have been far better to continue the retreat without stopping,” wrote Prince Wilhelm of Baden. “Many officers, calling on their last reserves of strength, would have reached the German frontier and would have been saved.” 

When it was time to leave he tried to persuade them to come with him, but after one night of release, these men who had come so far found they had the strength to go no further. “We had for some time been measuring out our forces in order to reach this city in which we believed we would find what we needed to satisfy our most imperious needs; rest, bread, and Vilna had come to form a trinity which was united in our minds as a single hope, and as a result we were clear in our minds that we would go no further than this city,” wrote Adrian de Mailly.

--

disaster ensues, some 10k-20k troops flee with Murat and Ney

they leave 20-30k behind in the city who were unable to move

The Russians arrive to what is basically "a frozen morgue"

most of the men left behind die from typhus, starvation, and hypothermia

the rest are killed or captured by Cossacks, with the locals joining in so they don't get attacked next

tens of thousands of French troops get buried in massive trenches, bodies which are still occasionally uncovered by construction workers today.

but the psychological breaking point is the part that is most fascinating to me, that stopping for rest was their downfall, and that they would have been better off continuing to march in the freezing cold on no rest

tells u something fascinating about the human spirit, and the ability to summon courage when most needed...

on "the eminent dead," Lyndon Johnson, power dynamics, respect, cunning, and manipulative behavior

"dead men tell no tales"

1/9

reason #1000 why u want to study the eminent dead, is because a lot of the most useful information as far as navigating society, politics, and "the ways of men"... is stuff that people will never admit to doing, for fear of being perceived as manipulative or cunning.

as always, the truth is nuanced...

when u study the past 2000 years of biography, history etc, u will see that men are the same in all eras

but then in real life, u will sometimes hit a divergence

"why doesn't this person fit the fact pattern that I know"

it's because they're on some straight-up bullshit lol

faking like turkey bacon

it's not always nefarious, sometimes men are forced by circumstance into a persona that just isn't them -- living a lie for years on end -- but as I will explain, this is why u have to study the dead ones.

over and over, people u know will reveal that they weren't who they seemed to be...and as a result, u have a head full of incorrect conclusions that u drew based on some Potemkin personality type.

2.

a few of the eminent dead who come to mind, there are men like LBJ who absolutely fit these adjectives (manipulative, deceitful, cunning) by nature, unapologetically so.

or Ben Franklin, or Talleyrand, pretty much any diplomat or politician who made it to the #1 seed, u can guarantee they're wired that way more than most.

but every single man is born with these traits in them, just to varying degrees.

think of any corporate setting you've ever been in, as a fly on the wall, watching human beings do what they do, and ask "how much of this is manipulative behavior"

all the sucking up and brown nosing, trying to appear to ppl a certain way

always thinking "I want to say X but I can't, so I'll say Y"

if it isn't the truth, there is manipulation involved

"white lies," all the hierarchy/power structure considerations, the way that you treat the CEO different than you treat a summer intern

this is all manipulative behavior even if u prefer to call it something nicer.

3.

the way people treat the intern is usually their true nature

which means the way u see them treating the CEO, or their boss... is almost entirely bullshit, manipulation, and cunning.

an honest man will be open about "I have engaged in this behavior," a dishonest man will say "everyone else does that stuff, except for me."

this tends to be a universal truth, and out of 100 ppl, may reveal the 2 or 3 who aren't completely full of shit.

additionally, it is almost impossible to know others, to know human nature, to know the ways of men and all their vices, while also lying to yourself about whether these same vices exist within you (hint: they do).

4.

either way, the goal here is to thread the needle

that means, first and foremost, becoming fluent in how all this shit works...all the social dynamics, from respect to power, so that u can "read the room" no matter where u are.

and then second, trying to embody all the positive traits that will get u what u want -- meaning u get rid of all "fake it til u make it," u consciously choose not to engage in any manipulative or cunning behavior, or anything that could even be perceived as such.

every action has both a selfless and a selfish motive

its good to acknowledge both, not just internally, but in dealing w/ others and putting all ur cards on the table

because when u hear a man claim he's driven by 100% pure altruism... 🚩🚩🚩

people are driven far more by selfish motives than selfless ones

this is just basic human nature, and it's the origin of Franklin's "appeal to interest and not to reason." Munger writes about this ad nauseum in the context of wrongdoing at Salomon Brothers.

5.

but here, the selfless motive of not "faking it til u make it" is that this is just a mark of good character, u are the same person 24/7.

at the same time, the selfish motive is that all manipulation and cunning will be detected by the people at the top (the #1 seed, CEO, whoever)

u dont get there and stay there unless u can read people.

from the outside, u will see others trying to "run game" on them, and while they appear to be falling for it, they operate on 3rd or 4th level thinking

i.e. "I'm going to let this person think they're manipulating me"

the gameplan being...bait them, let them drop their guard, and then let them overplay their hand.

now, they'll never admit to you, or to any other living soul, that this is how they operate. 

for two reasons.

first, to reveal the web would result in never catching another fly. this is the selfish motive.

second, as in the intro, this is the type of behavior that would be deemed manipulative, cunning, and perhaps shameful.

no living man wants to be known as those things, thus, he will deny it or lie about it until the day he dies

and this is yet another reason why you have to study dead men to learn the truth.

if u didn't understand what I meant at the start of this post, I think u should by now.

6.

point being, u can assume that the person who you want/need to like you...the one who is higher up...is someone that spends their entire day dealing with people who are 1000x better at bullshit, manipulation, and cunning than u are.

once again, the best way to win the game is to not play it at all.

so for me to say, "you should figure out who you need to like you, and then make them like you," would be horrible advice bc it's self-defeating.

they will see exactly what u are trying to do and it will backfire, because they will sense that you aren't being genuine in your intent.

7.

this is what I mean by thread the needle.

you probably want to be able to enter a room and understand, intuitively, who is respected and who isn't -- which u can learn from studying the Lyndon Johnson types

but beyond that, the middle ground isn't "what can I say to someone that will make them respect me"

it's, how can I be someone that they will naturally end up respecting?

and this tends to be the opposite route.

8.

they're going to be most curious about the person who is clearly courteous and respectful, but who isn't flattering them or treating them any different than they treat the summer intern.

this process, them viewing u as different from the rest, can only occur gradually, organically, and over long periods of time.

the other ppl thinking, "what 1x thing can I say/do to make them like me" -- this always fails.

some of the positive can be gained simply thru years of not engaging in the negative

but if I really had to put words to it, I'd phrase it as: "integrity has a way of leaking out."

9.

they're going to learn who u really are not thru direct observation, but from the 1000's of pieces of info they hear from others about their 1x1 interactions with u, behind closed doors.

honestly, someone high up will get the best read from talking to the summer intern

i.e. "who do you like here"

"oh, I like so-and-so the best, he spends a ton of time going out of his way to teach me shit, help me learn and answer my questions"

no one has anything to gain from the guy at the very bottom

and so thats why this guy provides a clearer read on someone's character, than the version that he sees each day presented to his face.

END/SUMMARY

this is not really an advice post, or one where I can guide u...as I said before, anything forced will be sensed as such, and the correct path is specific to who u are.

the operative Q to answer, is from the view of a fly on the wall: "if you were someone else, would you admire and respect you?"

and the best path to that is some mix of, "be genuine in ur intent" and "have a high degree of earned self-respect."

but to my knowledge, there is no way to achieve those things other than to be authentically yourself -- whoever that person may be.

everything else will fail.

the closest thing to a universal truth that u will find, directly observable in the ways of men, can be found in this quote by Samuel Johnson, and in my experience it has proved 100% accurate and reliable:

"The true measure of a man is how he treats someone who can do him absolutely no good."

for L/S, there is something to be gained in thinking about process the same way you'd think about a blackjack system

because u are taking lots of shots and relying on the law of large numbers -- over say 10,000 hands -- to where process and outcome should converge

(1/6) - this is especially true in multi-mgr where u might have 50 names, each of which present say 10 events/catalysts per year

so as an analyst, that's 500 shots

in blackjack, basic strategy reduces the house edge from 2-5% to less than 1%...basic strategy being the systematic model which dictates ur best move based on ur cards + the dealer upcard

and so in a L/S seat where ur taking tons of shots, u want to gradually strip out discretion where possible, in the quest to make ur process consistent and repeatable

even Buffett, despite being "qualitative" as a fundamental biz analyst, is pretty systematic in how he goes about shit. his decision making process is more akin to a gigabrained probability-calculation machine than a human being.

experience teaches u that there's a sliding scale of discretionary vs systematic, and esp in risk mgmt or sell discipline, u want to automate + remove emotion

but the exact calibration of the scale, the right % of discretion, that's a lifelong adjustment process and specific to u.

this is why blackjack is useful as a mental model. I think Munger prefers pari-mutuel betting/horseracing as the analogue, bc the payoffs are more reflective of how markets price assets, but both work (as does poker).

2.

as for the "basic strategy" of markets, it would be whatever mix of variables comprise winning process for u...no clear definition/many possible inputs.

i.e. understanding ur "circle of competence," ur style, and identifying the setups where u consistently are able to extract dollars from the market

lots of tiny details which u can only learn thru trial and error

but this is how ur odds improve from the standard 50-50 coin flip proposition

meaning...if u or me or a monkey throwing darts showed up, picked a random ticker, and blindly clicked "buy" or "sell," we theoretically should all begin with the same 50-50

3. 

the main difference is that in markets, u have a much wider variance in batting/slugging

some of the greatest managers ever, like Soros or PTJ, are only right 30-40% of the time

but their low win rate/batting average, is offset by their winners being much larger in size than their losers.

in simple numbers: if u can get a win rate of 51%, just north of even, and have your wins be 2x the size of your losses...u are going to be one of the greatest money managers of all time.

over 10,000 trades, ur annualized return/CAGR will be about 50%.

if u assume 1,000 trades per year, over 10 years your equity will 50x... $100,000 turns to $5 million.

4. 

will u have a 51% win rate, probably not

this is simply to illustrate that u only need a tiny edge + bigger wins than losses + large sample size, for a system to generate crazy LT returns.

if u assume a 40% win rate with the same ratio (reward = 2x risk), ur annualized return is 19% -- about the same as Buffett.

but if u reduce the ratio to 1.5x, meaning ur wins are 1.5x the size of ur losses, ur returns on a 40% hit rate collapse to breakeven (~0% annualized return).

u can fuck around with the math all u want, but the only way any of this becomes reality is by taking thousands and thousands of shots, year after year

this is the first step, figuring out where u have the highest hit rate, with the second step being risk mgmt, sell discipline, cutting losses fast and letting winners run

5.

the most important takeaway from all this, is that everything starts and ends with "breaking down tape"

u cannot know what ur good at without staring at ur historical P&L/trade blotter

and there have to be a lot of reps in there for signal to emerge from noise

so go pay ur "tuition," the only way u learn markets is thru thousands of reps and years of generating red P&L

until u have losses to study, u don't have shit

this all applies for building models as well. u gauge the efficacy of a model by whether it correctly forecasts earnings

if u arent measuring ur forecasts vs actual, measuring ur process vs the outcome, u are just wasting ur time

that's what the 2x2 matrix below is for -- process vs outcome -- those four possible squares encompass every trade or investment result, and they tell u where u need to devote ur time.

otherwise, u aren't iterating. nothing is getting done. u don't know what's luck and what's skill, and u really have no clue if what u are doing in general is right or dead wrong.

6.

above all, u gain absolutely nothing from scrolling twtr

scrolling only leads to ppl having 1,000 new ideas each day, software, oil, gold, and asking 1,000 dumb ass questions where I give the exact same answer:

"what does ur P&L say?"

all the answers u seek are in your red P&L

if u understand the self-improvement process via trial & error -- as in, take shots, analyze ur mistakes, iterate off them, and repeat -- there is a 0% chance u are DMing me or anyone else

none of us have a clue if u should buy software

u will only learn if u should, by doing it 100 times and studying ur P&L. everything is trial by fire

asking ppl about 1000 new trade ideas only says "I'm not serious about markets" or "I'm afraid of putting $ at risk" or something else that just feels wrong

either the hunger and the passion are missing, or the mind is just dialed to a different frequency.

END

before experience, there is def an attitude/mindset that is conducive for all this, and its visible at a young age

there is a lot of informational content in this quote from Steve Cohen on evaluating trader talent: "I'm looking for people who are not afraid to take risks. One of the questions I ask is: "Tell me some of the riskiest things you've ever done in your life." I want guys who have the confidence to be out there; to be risk takers."

that's exactly it...not specific to him at all, look at a Druck or Soros or Tepper, look at Buffett/Munger, all their track records are built off slugging + riding winners in monstrous stomach-churning size.

if u embrace risk, u will be dying to test ur ideas in the market with $ attached, or at least, ur competition will be

versus just going thru the motions of doing stock pitches and models, listening to business podcasts all day, reading too much business news, other pointless business bullshit with no tie to P&L

if u just want to "talk stocks" without any cost basis or P&L attached, then go tweet all day, that's what 99.9% of ppl are here for

but stop wasting ppl's time pretending like ur serious 

why would anyone want to critique pitches where u never have a single dollar behind any of them...if u have no conviction in ur ideas, if u clearly don't care, no one else is going to care either.

esp when ur competition consists of psychopath mf's who are foaming at the mouth

ultimately the best feedback u will get on a pitch will always come directly from the market -- particularly in the form of red P&L

so if u actually want to improve, take some risk for fucks sake

a man named jim simons has some advice for u...u may have heard it before, it's his #1 recommended way for someone to learn investing.

"Go short some wheat and see how it feels."

good luck trading

on reading habits... the way I'd break it down to my 23-year old self

arguably the most important thing to get right in determining the trajectory of ur life

1/5

first priority, u gotta master whatever is needed for work + reach the highest level of proficiency...this is not limitless, somewhere in the 5-10 year range u should be "finished"

lets say ur done with most work days at 7-8ish

on two or three weeknights, when u arent being social, u can knock out 1-2 hours of reading

go out friday night + either saturday day or sunday day, and block off the other day as "work" (usually sunday)

if ppl are out u say "I can't make it, I have to work," which is true in the sense of...ur working because u want to win. and reading always falls under the bucket of work

after u do whatever actual work u need to do, u knock out 3-5 hours reading

the compounding of these days, and weeknights, is what creates a massive difference over a decade

2/5

once u no longer suck at ur job / are done with that reading, u start mixing in stuff like top novels of all time, classics, history

but really u want to focus on "The Eminent Dead" as Munger calls them

great man bios, heroes, conquerors, leaders, all the way back to the Greeks and Romans

u want to build relationships with them, where u develop their collective voices in ur head, and let their advice be what guides u through life.

I didn't understand this until say 35 but it could've been useful at 25

3/5

uploading the "eminent dead" is how u become a leader and exercise independent judgement, rather than blindly following the crowd

u will quickly realize that most people have no fucking clue what they're doing, a lot of opinions are just mechanically repeating what they were told

if u ask ppl "why do u believe what u believe?" they freeze up

and in following the footsteps of the eminent dead, u will recognize that there is a wide divergence in what they would do vs. what the crowd u see around u is doing..."this isn't right, this isn't how all the heroes throughout history would act."

everything great comes from having courage in ur own convictions + from a willingness to say, "I see everyone going that way, but I know that the correct thing to do is go this way"

over time, people will pick up on that u have some clue what ur doing, and they will start following u

4/5

on social media, u mostly want to leave this shit alone

all it does is slopbeam "crowd habits" into ur brain rather than the habits of the eminent dead, which u would get from books

these forums are best used for getting "reps" in writing, in creativity, evaluating ur ideas, and getting feedback

stay as far away as possible from the gossip section, or passing judgment on random finance/tech "celebrities" who u will never meet and have no bearing on ur life

when ur young, u will see the crowd doing it and u will blindly do what the crowd does so u can "fit in"

u will make an anonymous account and talk about how stupid terry smith is, despite that he runs 12 billion, and ur unemployed daytrading a $25k robinhood account

as u read more u will see that the Eminent Dead are unanimous on critics...loathed, held in contempt, viewed as cowards, and criticism in general is viewed as a massive waste of time, i.e. "great minds talk about ideas, small minds talk about people"

when u look back at the time u spent engaging in it, u will realize they were right. u never gain anything in bringing others down, every single minute is an 100% pure waste of time 

u will learn that u can read people very quickly based on what they talk about, because people talk about what they think about, and people think about whatever they upload

for some that's books, for others its gossip

but for all, the output will always reflect the input... because "what you focus on expands."

5/5

as long as u block off these weekly hours, and u keep a stack of 10 books around, ur gonna be good

u can have several genres going - few novels, few bios, few history books, few psychology/philosophy, etc

because ur mood will change, ur attention span is variable, and some books require deeper concentration than others

biographies tend to be a heavier lift, whereas any novel written in the last 50 years... u can be tired and hungover and still rip through it

read what appeals to u, dont worry about what everyone else thinks, never force anything

some writers or individual titles inevitably just wont click for u

there's no rhyme or reason, I don't like Dickens, I don't like Dostoevsky, I like Tolstoy, I like some Thomas Mann, but not all....is this how it's "supposed" to be, I don't know and don't care

u read these books to try and figure out how this life shit actually works. there is no "supposed," a book is either helping u or it isnt

if one isn't working for u, just give it to a friend and keep starting new books until one "clicks," it always will

END

that's all there is to it

if u read a lot, u will never in your life know what "boredom" or "loneliness" feel like

every problem u will ever face, there is a book written on how to either solve it, or how to navigate it while keeping ur head about u

and if a book shifts ur worldview, and u suddenly recognize u have the wrong ppl around u, trust ur gut and change what needs to be changed

the eminent dead will never steer u wrong

John Adams defending British soldiers after the Boston Massacre in 1770 is one of those acts where u really have to question, would u have had the stones to do that

five ppl killed, murder charges, no lawyer in the city would risk taking the case for the British defense

Adams agrees to do it driven by belief in rule of law and the right to a fair trial, and to establish that the colonies had a functional system that wouldn't bend to politics

city turns on him, Adams loses half his legal practice, but argues that the soldiers were acting in self-defense against a riotous mob

six soldiers get acquitted, two get a lesser charge, none hanged

months later, Adams gets elected to the house of representatives, and later reflects on the case as "...one of the most gallant, generous, manly and disinterested actions of my whole life, and one of the best pieces of service I ever rendered to my country."

does the wise man make that choice, idk, there's a hundred ways it could have ended in disaster or death

but it was a high-risk bet that went in Adams' favor, and posterity now knows it as a defining act of courage...

final thoughts on this book, the art of memoir, and autobio

1/3. these are extremely hard to write well...about as high-risk/high-reward as u can get. 

the truth is that there is no way to write effectively about one's life, without speaking about life as it really was -- and that includes whatever took place involving the people around you.

in a good memoir or autobio, u know early on: "mfs must be HEATED that he wrote this."

this is unavoidable

and u can tell equally quickly, in the other direction, when a book has been whitewashed or when a man's life story doesn't ring true to, well, real life

the approach, which Agassi gets right, is "I’m going to hold myself accountable first and foremost."

Others are a distant second to that, but if you are brutally honest and harsh on your own conduct, and show true courage in tearing yourself down, it becomes much harder for ppl to push back when they get a lesser version of that same treatment.

because the truth is the truth. what happened, happened, and if you don't like what you said or did, perhaps you shouldn't have said or done it in the first place?

there is an enormous amount of tact involved here in knowing what to include vs exclude, and you don't want to bring other people's past into it unless absolutely necessary...but there is no way to recount a life, that doesn't include others.

and Agassi is just as complementary of some players (Federer) as he is negative of others (Chang, Becker, sometimes Sampras).

overall, Agassi/Moehringer nailed the balance here

2/3. this is a true self-help book

"self-help" is a horseshit category, most of what u see that is new or on twtr, is recycling other people's wisdom, or trying to share the lessons of another man's hardship story

the issue is that it rings hollow immediately

if the hardest thing you've ever been through is "I was disillusioned by my finance job," the writing is going to be awful...u can def sell a few copies but the book will be forgotten in less than a year

true heroism, true self-help, is to pull a mirror out and show the world the ugliest sides of yourself

the reader will examine their own flaws accordingly, in private, and this is how you get another man to change.

3/3. no explaining, no neat packaging

the last thing this book does exceptionally well, is it doesn't feel the need to explain, to rationalize one's behavior, or conclude everything with a neat lesson about life

life is messy

a book about life should be messy, it should just vomit pain and suffering, bleeding out for the reader and saying "here"

if its too neat its fugazi

if you've read any of Trump's books, this is the flaw they all suffer from...there's bits of wisdom, but he's mostly trying to paint a picture of himself. he wants to portray an image and the writing suffers as a result

same issue with Rousseau's "Confessions" and many other autobios

the way you write a really good one of these books, is to tell how you felt AT THAT TIME.  not how you feel today, about what happened back then.

this is extraordinarily difficult and means unpacking and unwiring your brain, wading through the primordial soup of memory

and the lessons here are presented in a way that isn't mawkish or overly sentimental...very hard to understand what he means here, unless you've been there, in which case you recognize it as 100% truth:

“I know for sure that there's pain in life. We have to fight through our pain and find a way to get through it. Life is about fighting through that pain and, when you can, easing the pain of others.”

END

quotedTweet.text:
incredible book from 2009...kept seeing this on "best autobios ever" lists, almost looked out of place, but it isnt.

much credit due to co-author J.R. Moehringer who is just a dazzingly good writer, a master hand, one of the best I can remember coming across

the two of them, plus the entire team that helped put this together, transcended the genre...really isn't a sports book or tennis book at all, it covers the following topics as well as anything I've ever read:

-self-mastery/knowledge of self...the three enemies, the game + the opponent + the self: this applies for pretty much any endeavor but you have the game (in this case, say, swinging a racket). 

then you have the opponent who you are playing, sometimes even moreso than the game -- boxing, poker come to mind. 

finally, you have you against YOURSELF. you can know the game and know your opponent ice cold...but if u aren't master of self, and if u cant execute, all that other shit doesnt matter...u are ur own worst enemy.

I think of this a lot bc people see all these book recs (whether markets or otherwise), esp if younger, and are like "what order should I tackle these"

by laying it out as 3 enemies...it makes a little more sense

-"swinging the racket," the game, has to be #1, those are the fundamentals. master those first
-"know thy opponent" is second...this is more, understanding human nature and psychological/emotional biases
-"know thyself" is third and final, the hardest and the lifelong one

u cant qualify for the US Open if u cant swing the racket

then, u have all players studying one another's weaknesses

but when it comes down to the final...like agassi/sampras, its gonna come down to who is "master of self"

amazing quote in there: "the fifth set has nothing to do with tennis."

entirely about breaking your opponent's will, conditioning...stuff u see in all sports, momentum, like where your opponent throws their absolute best stuff, and u take it and ur still standing

thats when u see the look in their face, thats when u know they are broken

and thats when u smoke their fucking boots.

-success/failure 2x...internal/external...how hollow victory is, how all pain is 2x any victory: King Solomon-esque, and a ton of credit is due to Moehringer here

these are extremely complex topics to handle well and he shapes Agassi's story into these sort of eternal frameworks

the notion that, the entire world can view you as a success, ranked #1 in the world, but you look in the mirror and all you see is failure...you feel nothing

and then at the bottom when the world sees u as a failure but u dont feel that way at all

almost 0 correlation between this 4-way "mirror" for lack of a better word (success/failure/internal/external), a theme u see over and over in amazing stories like these...the way u feel abt urself is laughably disconnected from the way the world feels about you

and then the pain of failure far exceeding the thrill of victory...something u see over and over as well

losing in the finals of a slam, hurts 2x as bad as winning a slam feels

but you see this in so many other books that its not tennis specific, thats what I mean by how the book transcends the genre...tons in here directly applicable to markets, same way if u were to ask "what was jiro dreams of sushi" about, u know sushi is the absolute last thing.

more later, I rarely take notes while reading but this one had me going...tons of screenshots of quotes/excerpts....I don't think any book is a 10/10, but for the autobio genre, this is as close to a 10/10 as u will find.

art, not science...better to be vaguely right than precisely wrong

but with a lot of ideas, ppl don't understand the bet they're making

i.e. "I like exxon mobil" without thinking about:

>what % of your return will be driven by the price of oil?
>why exxon vs any other peer?
>if you're bullish oil, why wouldn't u make the cleanest bet and just buy a barrel of oil/CL1?

then u might get into, "I like exxon but don't want to bet on oil, so I'll short chevron against it to hedge out commodity exposure"

but in practice, unless u really know what ur doing, this creates more problems than it solves

esp w/ rise of multi-mgr where everyone is forced into pairs

so rather than adding complexity to the idea u are prob better off pulling out all the embedded/hidden bets u are making, and then just breaking it all down thru some checklist, like:

"would I be better off here buying a basket of 5 ideas, 2% each, vs one 10% idea"

"for this idea shifting industry dynamics, why don't I buy all 3 players" instead of bucketing one idea as "pay up for best" or "buy cheapest" or "buy middle/catch-up trade"

tweets.text:
"Go where there's dumb competition" is one of the better Mungerisms, but harder to put in practice than it sounds...few points of nuance

1. if you were to look for the dumbest competition, logic would say, look for a 'know-nothing' neophyte slash retail/casual investor, and then take the other side of their trade

right off the bat, that means you're on the short side, which puts you at a severe disadvantage just bc of the "in practice" considerations (position sizing, risk/reward, max payoff vs max loss)

you can try and invert this, but there really are no "dumb" short sellers...they're forced into higher levels of homework to offset the practical disadvantages above

2. a lot of times, the 'know-nothing' investor, they are chasing what are basically levered equity stubs or OTM call options

the expected value will be negative, say a 0.1% chance of 10x'ing vs. 99.9% chance it goes to zero.

but in practice, u can't take that risk, something like gamestop or a fartcoin can nuke ur account and end ur career.

that's why "go where there's dumb competition" doesn't really work

3. the best inversion of this, in practice, would be "don't go where there's smart competition."

today, that usually translates to: "am I going up against BAM/MLP/P72 etc in this trade idea?"

simplest definition of that, would be..."am I playing for a discrete/binary catalyst on a sub-3 month time horizon?"

because that's their game...u have literally sought out the toughest possible competition.

worth applying as a filter for any/all ideas u see, on here or otherwise, bc u will recognize - "wow u could not have picked a worse poker table to sit at."

(END)

A: I wouldn’t go where the big boys have to be, trying to decide whether Merck’s pipeline is better than Pfizer’s. I’d go where there are market inefficiencies and your work could lead to knowing important things that other people didn’t.

so my first reply to the BAH pitch was, pull up price charts of all the peers and you can see it pretty fast (below)...you aren't making an idiosyncratic bet

the bet might be right (maybe BAH is okay and ACN isnt) but you gotta understand what battle you're fighting

your idea isn't down in a vacuum, its not "cheap bc its complex" or something tied to the biz in question, u have to understand + debunk the broad AI/LLM bear case

thats why these situations are hard, not just bc those are tough to debunk, but then you have to lay out "what is the event path/specific catalysts that will make the market view change + arrive at my variant view"

a lot of times, beating the next 2-3 qtrs doesn't change shit, bc that's not where the mkt is looking on the DCF...it knows 12-24 mo FCF is fine, it's concerned about "are LT EBIT margins 10% or 5%" or "is perp growth 5%, 0%, or (5%)?"

I have no opinion on whether these are the right battles to fight, but I don't think there's anything wrong with saying "fuck this" or tossing it into the "too hard" pile once u realize an idea is not what u thought it was.

incredible book from 2009...kept seeing this on "best autobios ever" lists, almost looked out of place, but it isnt.

much credit due to co-author J.R. Moehringer who is just a dazzingly good writer, a master hand, one of the best I can remember coming across

the two of them, plus the entire team that helped put this together, transcended the genre...really isn't a sports book or tennis book at all, it covers the following topics as well as anything I've ever read:

-self-mastery/knowledge of self...the three enemies, the game + the opponent + the self: this applies for pretty much any endeavor but you have the game (in this case, say, swinging a racket). 

then you have the opponent who you are playing, sometimes even moreso than the game -- boxing, poker come to mind. 

finally, you have you against YOURSELF. you can know the game and know your opponent ice cold...but if u aren't master of self, and if u cant execute, all that other shit doesnt matter...u are ur own worst enemy.

I think of this a lot bc people see all these book recs (whether markets or otherwise), esp if younger, and are like "what order should I tackle these"

by laying it out as 3 enemies...it makes a little more sense

-"swinging the racket," the game, has to be #1, those are the fundamentals. master those first
-"know thy opponent" is second...this is more, understanding human nature and psychological/emotional biases
-"know thyself" is third and final, the hardest and the lifelong one

u cant qualify for the US Open if u cant swing the racket

then, u have all players studying one another's weaknesses

but when it comes down to the final...like agassi/sampras, its gonna come down to who is "master of self"

amazing quote in there: "the fifth set has nothing to do with tennis."

entirely about breaking your opponent's will, conditioning...stuff u see in all sports, momentum, like where your opponent throws their absolute best stuff, and u take it and ur still standing

thats when u see the look in their face, thats when u know they are broken

and thats when u smoke their fucking boots.

-success/failure 2x...internal/external...how hollow victory is, how all pain is 2x any victory: King Solomon-esque, and a ton of credit is due to Moehringer here

these are extremely complex topics to handle well and he shapes Agassi's story into these sort of eternal frameworks

the notion that, the entire world can view you as a success, ranked #1 in the world, but you look in the mirror and all you see is failure...you feel nothing

and then at the bottom when the world sees u as a failure but u dont feel that way at all

almost 0 correlation between this 4-way "mirror" for lack of a better word (success/failure/internal/external), a theme u see over and over in amazing stories like these...the way u feel abt urself is laughably disconnected from the way the world feels about you

and then the pain of failure far exceeding the thrill of victory...something u see over and over as well

losing in the finals of a slam, hurts 2x as bad as winning a slam feels

but you see this in so many other books that its not tennis specific, thats what I mean by how the book transcends the genre...tons in here directly applicable to markets, same way if u were to ask "what was jiro dreams of sushi" about, u know sushi is the absolute last thing.

more later, I rarely take notes while reading but this one had me going...tons of screenshots of quotes/excerpts....I don't think any book is a 10/10, but for the autobio genre, this is as close to a 10/10 as u will find.

(Lewis Borsellino, ex-Merc S&P futures trader)

Introduction 

In the 20 years I’ve been trading, I’ve discovered one truism that is valid whether you’re trading stocks, fixed income or futures: trading is 90% psychological. All the rest – technical analysis, trade execution, etc. – is the other 10%.

That’s not to say that technical analysis of the markets isn’t important. It’s vital. You can’t trade without a plan based on technical analysis that encompasses support and resistance, trend lines, moving averages, momentum, volatility and the like. But you can’t possibly execute that plan consistently if your mental game is off. That’s where the ‘ten commandments’ of trading come in. 

(from Jenks - 'Harriman Book of Investing')

1. Trade for success, not for money. 

Your motivation should be first and foremost to make a well-executed trade. If money alone is your motivation you will severely limit your chance of success. Why? Because focusing on money will raise all kinds of emotional issues, from fear to greed. It will make you afraid of losses to the point that you will abandon your discipline. It will tempt you to trade too often, too large and with too much risk. Whereas if you focus on making solid, well- executed trades - even if the result is a losing trade that you exit quickly - you will reinforce your discipline and increase your trading potential.

2. Discipline is the one quality that all traders must possess above all others. 

The ability to master your mind, your body and your emotions is the key to trading. The disciplined trader - regardless of profit or loss - comes back to trade another day. A great intellect, the ability to take on risk, or even a sense that you’re somehow ‘lucky’ mean nothing without discipline. For a trader, discipline means the ability to devise a trading plan, execute according to that plan, and to never deviate from that plan. 

3. Know yourself. 

Do you break out in a cold sweat at the mere thought of risking something - such as your own capital? Do you think of trading like ‘gambling,’ a long shot to make a million? Or can you handle risk in a disciplined fashion, knowing how much is ‘too much’ for both your capital and your constitution? Trading is not for everyone. If risk makes you ill, on the one hand, or if taking a risk brings out the recklessness in you, then trading is probably not for you. But if you can handle risk with discipline, then perhaps you can find a vocation or avocation as a trader. Only you can answer that question. 

4. Lose your ego. 

No matter how much success you enjoy as a trader, you’ll never outsmart the market. If you think you can, you’re in for a very humbling experience. The market rules, always, and for everyone. You need to silence your ego in order to listen to the market, to follow what your technical analysis is indicating - and not what your intellect (and your ego) think should happen. To trade effectively, you need to put yourself aside. At the same time, you cannot be so emotionally fragile that unprofitable trades shatter your confidence. Don’t be crushed by the market, but don’t ever think you’ve mastered it, either. 

5. There’s no such thing as hoping, wishing or praying. 

I’ve seen too many traders staring panic-stricken at the computer screen and begging the market to move their way. Why? Because they have lost their discipline and allowed what was a small loss to turn into a much bigger one. They keep hanging on, hoping, wishing and praying for things to turn around. The reality is on the screen. When the market hits your stop-loss level (the price at which you’ll cut your losses at a pre-determined level), get out.

6. Let your profits run and cut your losses quickly. 

When the market goes against you and you hit your pre-determined stop, exit the trade. Period. Exit when the loss is a small one. Then reevaluate your strategy and execute a new trade. Keeping your losses small will keep you in the game. Profits take care of themselves, as long as you execute according to your plan. When you place a trade, know in advance where you’ll exit for a profit. When the market reaches that level, exit the position. If your technical analysis tells you the market still has some room to move, then scale out of the position. But execute according to your plan. Remember, you’ll never go broke taking a profit. 

7. Know when to trade and when to wait. 

Trade when your analysis, your system and your strategy say that you have a buy or sell to execute. If the market doesn’t have a clear direction, then wait on the sidelines until it does. Keep your mind on the market, but keep your money out of it. 

8. Love your losers like you love your winners. 

Losing trades will be your best teachers. When you have a losing trade, it’s because of some flaw in your analysis or your judgment. Or perhaps the market simply didn’t do what you thought it would. When you have a losing trade, something is out of sync with the market. Examine what went wrong - objectively - then adjust your thinking, if necessary, and enter the trade again. 

9. After three losing trades in a row, take a break.

This is not the time to take on more risk, but rather to become extremely disciplined. Sit on the sidelines for a while. Watch the market. Clear your head. Re-evaluate your strategy, and then put on another trade. Losses can shake your confidence and tempt you to become emotional (fear/greed) But if you take a break, you can gather your wits and regain your composure more quickly than if you become very emotional and angry at yourself and the market. 

10. The unbreakable rule. 

You can break a rule and get away with it once in a while. But one day, the rules will break you. If you continually violate these ‘commandments’ of trading, you will eventually pay for it with your profits. That’s the unbreakable rule. If you have trouble with any of them, come back and read this one. Then read it again.

there's an inverse version of this post - "common investing and market maxims that fail to hold."

two that come to mind (and many more will) are "tops are a process, bottoms are an event" and "buy blood in the streets / be greedy when others are fearful"

its not that any of these maxims are outright wrong -- they survive for a reason -- but they are often misapplied or have nuance that needs to be given

the 2nd one is simpler so we'll start there. what happens is that since it came from Buffett, people take it and then just average down over and over in total piece of shit stocks

"buy blood," "greedy when fearful"

the truth is that until u are an advanced-level investor, or at least have several years of experience, u are prob better off being fearful when others are fearful

or at the very minimum, assume that his advice should be applied strictly to the S&P 500

capitalism is vicious and most businesses fail

I don't want to argue back-and-forth on this one but we can agree that 1. its frequently misapplied, and 2. has blown a shitload of accounts...the idea of being contrarian for contrarian sake, or that "down 90%" = "buy"

--

on "tops as a process, bottoms are an event"

this is semi-true

tops are a process but they are literally impossible to forecast/time...ask anyone who has been trading mkts for a long time and they'll agree, NO ONE with real P&L attached ever nails the top...the whole exercise is bigly negative on an expected value basis

peter lynch's "more $ has been lost trying to prepare for recessions, than in recessions themselves" is the best maxim for tops

tops are sneaky as fuck and quite often, even when its obvious shit is bubbly, things progress another 1-3 years...and a lot of times the biggest gains are at the end

so you're trying to dodge down 20%-30%, and miss the up 50-100%.  plus when ppl call "top," they exit and their mind locks them out, they never get back in...hence from the QT "no one is more bearish than a sold out bull."

a fun exercise (one that LLMs can prob help with) - for any top, pull the major news sources (WSJ/BBG etc) and read the daily headlines from top date plus/minus 4 weeks in each direction...get a feel for what the tone and sentiment was, upload to subconscious, may come in handy someday.

then, on bottoms being an event...this is almost never true.

you can have more luck timing bottoms than u can tops, but go study charts urself, u will see its never what people expect

the "event" resembling, a massive capitulation spike low, huge vomit, price-insensitive selling, gigantic volume, etc

these never turn out to be the bottom -- too obvious -- markets are way too cunning.

from a chart standpoint, the SPX in 2008-2009 is what bottoms usually look like (all of this being my humble and frequently-wrong opinion of course) -- I added the chart below

you had the big vomit in oct 2008, the blood in the streets, the "bottoms are an event"

so people bought, you got the oversold bounce, and then from Oct 2008 to March 2009....the SPX went down another 30% or so

more than anything else, bottoms are marked by APATHY.

every bottom I have ever seen or traded, in a stock or an index, it was always apathy bordering on despair or futility

lost track how many times I had this exact exchange on IB with someone:

me: "are you buying"

them: "no, it only goes down" or "no, I bought the spike low then got stopped out 10% lower, fuck this thing...you?"

me: "exact same thought"

and that very day... was always the bottom. seared into my memory each time

so the context/nuance I'd add, is that all the violence means you're probably CLOSE to a bottom...but not only could the bottom be another 30% away, bottoms are not guaranteed to be V-shaped

especially in individual stocks, sometimes a bottom is years long

the stock is bombed out and not going down any further, it ran out of sellers, but that doesnt mean it magically goes up...something has to change the narrative

and you have to factor in trade duration/opportunity cost of capital

it may be "10% down, 50% up," but having $ tied up earning 0% for years isn't a win when the mkt return is 7-8%

so "value is its own catalyst," sometimes true, sometimes not...the duration of the investment affects whether that's wise or not.

--

there's a lot more of these flawed maxims / ones that are hazardous on a standalone basis

but short term, the top maxims in the QT always seem to be the best go-to, almost Occam's razor-y

the big-brain backfitted answers from media and sales/trading desks always are secondary to stuff like:

"why was GOOG down the most yday," bc everyone's long
"why does the tape suck," bc incrementally hawkish fed

there's never an 100% correct answer but the closest thing to it is, fundamentals are always secondary to "max pain to max # of ppl" and "fed policy/liquidity drives everything."

remember, they still don't know what caused the crash of 1987...so, they prob don't know why the nasdaq was off 150 bps yesterday.

no one knows shit

good luck trading

this is by far the best answer I've seen to "why is intelligence is an impediment to successful trading?"

from Victor Sperandeo in Schwager -- every word here is a perfect 10/10.

"Besides trading, there is probably no other profession where you have to admit when you're wrong."

-----

Q: Was there any correlation between intelligence and success at trading?

"Absolutely, but not in the way you think. For example, one of the people I picked was a high school dropout, who I'm sure didn't even know the alphabet. He was one of the five who made me a great deal of money.

"He was my phone clerk on the American Stock Exchange, and he was very aggressive and alert. Also, he had been in Vietnam and had a hand grenade explode near him, leaving shrapnel in his pancreas. As a result of this experience, he was always afraid of everything. When it came to trading, he was more worried about losing than winning. He took losses very quickly. 

On the other extreme of the intelligence spectrum, one of the people I trained was a genius. He had a 188 IQ, and he was on "Jeopardy" once and answered every question correctly. That same person never made a dime in trading during five years."

"I discovered that you can't train people how to trade by just imparting knowledge. The key to trading success is emotional discipline. Making money has nothing to do with intelligence. Think of all the bright people that choose careers on Wall Street. If intelligence were the key, there would be a lot more people making money trading."

---

Q: You almost seem to be implying that intelligence is an impediment to successful trading. How would you explain that? 

"Assume that you're a brilliant student who graduates Harvard summa cum laude. You get a job with a top investment house, and within one year, they hand you a $5 million portfolio to manage. 

What would you believe about yourself? Most likely, you would assume that you're very bright and do everything right. Now, assume you find yourself in a situation where the market is going against your position. What is your reaction likely to be? "I'm right." Why? Because everything you've done in life is right. You'll tend to place your IQ above the market action. 

To be a successful trader, you have to be able to admit mistakes. People who are very bright don't make very many mistakes. In a sense, they generally are correct. In trading, however, me person who can easily admit to being wrong is the one who walks away a winner. 

Besides trading, there is probably no other profession where you have to admit when you're wrong. Think about it. For example, consider a lawyer who, right before a big case, goes out with his girlfriend and stays up half the night. The next day, he's drowsy and inadequately prepared. He ends up losing the case. Do you think he's going to tell the client, "I'm sorry, I went out last night and stayed up too long. If I were sharper, I would have won the case. Here's your money back." It will never happen. He can always find some excuse. He would probably say something like, "I did the best I could, but the jury was biased." He will never have to admit he was wrong. No one will ever know the truth except him. In fact, he'll probably push the truth so far into his subconscious that he'll never admit to himself that his own actions caused the loss of me case. 

In trading, you can't hide your failures. Your equity provides a daily reflection of your performance. The trader who tries to blame his losses on external events will never learn from his mistakes. For a trader, rationalization is a guaranteed road to ultimate failure.

quotedTweet.text:
checklist detail:

"The most famous short sellers in recent years were the Feshbach Brothers: Kurt, twins Joe and Matt, and non-Feshbach Tom Barton. Feshbach Brothers, founded in 1982, was the first group formed to concentrate on short selling. At the height of their funds in 1990, they managed more money by a significant factor than any competitor, with $600 million in individual, institutional, and pension fund money."

The Feshbachs looked for terminal shorts with these four characteristics: 

(source: "The Art of Short Selling" by Staley)

1. Stock prices overvalued by at least two times Feshbach perceived valuation.

2. A fundamental problem at the company.

3. A weak financial condition: working capital problems or high long-term debt, for example. 

4. Weak or crooked management.

The Feshbachs' keystone is intense work and, sometimes, informational overkill. They start with fundamental methods of analysis and overlay that process with information gathering from a wide range of sources.

The Feshbachs do not short a stock unless they expect it to decline in price by 50 percent, because they believe that the risk of short selling is too great for marginal plays. "We short stocks where the negatives so overwhelm the positives that, over time, the market can't just shrug off the bad news - eventually the stock price will reflect it," Joe says.

The Feshbachs do not find company visits or Wall Street analysts productive ways to gather information. 

Talks with management are not fruitful: "The company didn't get to be a good short without management's help." 

Wall Street is no help: "That's the place to get the bull story, not the bear story. The bias negates their usefulness to us in a lot of incidents."

The most difficult part of short selling is timing, and the Feshbachs do not presume to have an answer to what determines the optimal trigger point. Joe uses the example of CopyTele: What is an appropriate indicator that the stock is finally ready to give up the ghost? (CopyTele has no earnings or revenues and only the promise of a product.)

They believe that to sell short you have to be certain that you see an important factor that other people do not see. "But," Feshbach continues, "it's not enough to see it if it doesn't make a difference in the way the company is ultimately valued. You have to see those mechanics begin to impact the income statement and the balance sheet." 

You have to visualize how the change evolves through the health of the company. The Feshbachs feel that talking to competitors and suppliers reveals the climate and how long it might continue and gives insight into possible triggers. 

Joe Feshbach says, "You look for something that is obviously misperceived, obviously important, and obviously detrimental. At that point, if you're comfortable that it's already started to happen, that it's not discounted in the price, and that it is substantial enough to get you to the price target, then you ought to get started." 

He cautions that the first position is not necessarily the biggest because stocks go up and you want to be able to average up. But the time you really want to add to the position is when those factors become overwhelmingly apparent and the stock is still up."

tweets.text:
checklist detail:

"The most famous short sellers in recent years were the Feshbach Brothers: Kurt, twins Joe and Matt, and non-Feshbach Tom Barton. Feshbach Brothers, founded in 1982, was the first group formed to concentrate on short selling. At the height of their funds in 1990, they managed more money by a significant factor than any competitor, with $600 million in individual, institutional, and pension fund money."

The Feshbachs looked for terminal shorts with these four characteristics: 

(source: "The Art of Short Selling" by Staley)

1. Stock prices overvalued by at least two times Feshbach perceived valuation.

2. A fundamental problem at the company.

3. A weak financial condition: working capital problems or high long-term debt, for example. 

4. Weak or crooked management.

The Feshbachs' keystone is intense work and, sometimes, informational overkill. They start with fundamental methods of analysis and overlay that process with information gathering from a wide range of sources.

The Feshbachs do not short a stock unless they expect it to decline in price by 50 percent, because they believe that the risk of short selling is too great for marginal plays. "We short stocks where the negatives so overwhelm the positives that, over time, the market can't just shrug off the bad news - eventually the stock price will reflect it," Joe says.

The Feshbachs do not find company visits or Wall Street analysts productive ways to gather information. 

Talks with management are not fruitful: "The company didn't get to be a good short without management's help." 

Wall Street is no help: "That's the place to get the bull story, not the bear story. The bias negates their usefulness to us in a lot of incidents."

The most difficult part of short selling is timing, and the Feshbachs do not presume to have an answer to what determines the optimal trigger point. Joe uses the example of CopyTele: What is an appropriate indicator that the stock is finally ready to give up the ghost? (CopyTele has no earnings or revenues and only the promise of a product.)

They believe that to sell short you have to be certain that you see an important factor that other people do not see. "But," Feshbach continues, "it's not enough to see it if it doesn't make a difference in the way the company is ultimately valued. You have to see those mechanics begin to impact the income statement and the balance sheet." 

You have to visualize how the change evolves through the health of the company. The Feshbachs feel that talking to competitors and suppliers reveals the climate and how long it might continue and gives insight into possible triggers. 

Joe Feshbach says, "You look for something that is obviously misperceived, obviously important, and obviously detrimental. At that point, if you're comfortable that it's already started to happen, that it's not discounted in the price, and that it is substantial enough to get you to the price target, then you ought to get started." 

He cautions that the first position is not necessarily the biggest because stocks go up and you want to be able to average up. But the time you really want to add to the position is when those factors become overwhelmingly apparent and the stock is still up."

there's a term "mañana stocks," with credit due to a short-seller named Robert Wilson, as situations to avoid:

--

"Good short-sellers always ask: "What is the catalyst, when and where is the train wreck?" Bob Wilson, the famous and now-retired short-seller, always refused to short what he called "mañana stocks."

The subject company definitely is going to do something marvelous "mañana" or at some other ill-defined time in the future.

The silliest ideas in the world always have their hard core of true believers. When true believers find out that their beliefs have been challenged in the stock market by short-sellers (bears), they go wild and the result is often an unpleasant financial and psychological battle. 

True believers are bulls, and stock market bulls react to a rising short interest in their favorite stocks the way real bulls react to the matador's red muleta. Unless there is some inescapable reality to be faced at some clearly defined point down the road, these battles go on until both sides are exhausted. 

In short, do not short mañana stocks; short only those where you are convinced the day of judgment is near."
