Risk Management/Trading: Reading Material

These two terms are really synonymous...trading = managing risk.

I can't even think of what "non-risk management trading" would be

Trading is protecting the P&L. 

Giving back $1M on a winner and losing $1M on a loser are the same P&L of $1M, and represent the same poor management of risk, or failure to take profits, et cetera.

Books/Specific Interviews

This is strange but the best interviews on risk management that I've ever read, are consistently from commodity traders or ex-commodity traders.

And I say that from an equity analyst perspective. They are the most disciplined loss cutters.

From Market Wizards: the Kovner and Seykota interviews and others (Eckhardt), plus anything with PTJ of course.

I'm not huge on blogs/videos/podcast so I'm sure there's tons of "3 hour PTJ interviews," but the Return on Time is atrocious on all these.

You're looking for actionable insight you can use in your process, there might be 5 minutes in there. These two were pretty dense with good information: 

https://t.co/NHDUpHmk30

https://t.co/I7MhVKLE1L

Series/Titles: Market Wizards, John Train's books, Inside the House of Money

Basically, anything by Schwager, Train, or Drobny should fit the bill...they consistently do good work. They are the "core" of this genre.

Beyond that?

There is really not that much. 

I was just pinging LLM's and the titles they are suggesting are straight trash.

Part of this post is simply: do not waste time on these secondary/tertiary "trading" recommendations (Howard Marks? Taleb?) or historical non-fiction "risk management" about some bank that blew up.

None of this will help you become a better trader or risk manager, it would be like reading Liar's Poker it has a trading desk in it.

Once you read some of those OG market wizard guys, like Kovner, you will see what actual trading/risk management commentary looks like.

A lot of the memoirs I've read, I wouldn't demand that you use your time on them. Poor Return on Time, minimal actionable insight.

The Lefevre book on Jesse Livermore is a classic and should probably be on here, but the highlights will be in an LLM....you'll get 99% of the info and save 99% of the time.

Psychologists: May as well add everything by Mark Douglas and Ari Kiev here, it's trading-adjacent but it's psychology.

--

That's the end of the list. 

Feel free to reply or DM titles but I just vetted all the LLMs pretty heavily, and none of it is worth your time on a relative/opportunity cost basis.

Meaning, I'm benchmarking these books to, you spending time on something like Mauboussin or Buffett, or the other titles in my pinned tweet.

Beyond that, I have loose thoughts in these articles which are most useful in laying out, here are the various schools of thought available to you.

good luck trading,
GB

think it's axiomatic that pain increases ur tolerance for future pain

meaning, thick skin, so adversity seems to feel lighter

but I think what really happens, is u look back at all the good that came from bad outcomes in the past.

and u recognize that none of it could have been known ex ante.

so then the next time u get smashed by something completely senseless, tragic, and almost laughably random

you know that to search for divine design is pointless.

why?

because it has only appeared with the benefit of hindsight.

that's the benefit of experience, that's as far as you need to go in asking "why."

in these situations u are best off just shutting ur brain down. 

otherwise u go down a rabbithole of all the good you've done recently, and u feel some divine injustice, as if a good outcome was promised to you.

this causes u to question all ur beliefs, the idea that life is fair when it feels so unfair to you, and you're just in a state of agita which no man has ever been able to permanently settle.

so instead of doing all that, u block and tackle and go with what u know has worked.

u shrug and u say,

"I'll figure it out," because u always have.

u say,

"I don't know what good will come of this, but something will," because it always has.

and as an ex-military friend is quite fond of saying,

"shit makes great fertilizer."

trust in the divine presence, and know that u will only see it in the rearview.
 
off u go kiddo 🫡

two actions to be perfected

1. saying "I fucked up" at work
2. cutting a loss in trading

both need to become automatic...subconscious, like breathing

because you'll be doing them damn near every day until you die

this was a good question

re: "the market is always right" in #8

"I hate that comment, 'the market is wrong here.' The market is never wrong. When you own a stock that you think is worth X and is trading half of X, you're wrong. Something is missing. You find out later what it was. The market is always right and it tells you it is right." 

the full quote is below, manager named effron

so, this is clearly nuanced and there's no right answer, just schools of thought

boils down to: do u see red as risk, or red as opportunity...is down 20% "drawdown" or "back the truck up."

there are brilliant investors on both sides

the quote to me, I view as a default position/way of operating

and to me, this pairs with Buffett's 20 hole punchcard

you are not as smart as you think, you don't have as many good ideas as you think, overconfidence bias

everything re: efficiency is correct, but its the frequency of finding "opportunities" that is debated

most people don't do enough work to understand the market-implied/consensus view

they just see a stock that seems cheap

lot of times, stocks have taken a rocky road...there's damage to mgmt credibility, questionable margin flow-thru, no fcf, stocks have narratives and overhangs which affect why they are where they are.

if you are a sharp analyst who does real work, a lot of the time your correct conclusion after months of research should be, "its fairly priced"

not "I need ideas, and I just spent months on this, so its a long or a short"...which is what ends up happening.

biases/errors at work, now u have $ in a coin-flip bet, fairly valued stock, bc u couldnt just say the market had it right.

so as a default way of operating -- "mkt is right" as null hypothesis -- generating a new idea requires real effort, u have a lot to disprove for it to be a long or short

ur not just wandering into shit

and then the quote "if you say its worth X and its trading half X, you're wrong" -- out of 100 times, probably 90-95 of those, the quote is gonna be spot on

its not either/or (is the mkt efficient or inefficient) -- its understanding how rare a truly mispriced bet is, then sizing it, and then I think druck has a quote (along the lines of "invest first, investigate later") to the extent of.... shit only stays mispriced for 2-3 months. you have to move fast and with incomplete information.

as a rule of thumb, I think "actionable ideas generated" runs inverse with experience... a new trader has 500 ideas a day, a guy with 30 years experience sits on his hands all day, doing nothing, waiting for the perfect setup.

on man's penchant for total self-destruction

always notable to me how a man has one thing go wrong, then it inevitably kicks off a death spiral

which accelerates into BITFD mode, burn it the fuck down

and the spiral only ends, when everything is gone.

1/5

this is also known as "rock bottom"

u cannot lose more. u legitimately have nothing more left to lose.

this also happens to be the short answer to, "I know someone spiraling towards rock bottom, what can I do"

nothing

be there for them when they hit bottom

until then, get out of the way. there is a process in motion that the rest of the world is powerless to stop.

2/5

the way I was thinking about this, is that a man is a city

each building represents some facet of his life

job, family, money, shit like that

one building falls. 

we'll say he gets wiped out financially, some stablecoin or dumbass crypto trade.

he's stunned, hasn't told anyone.

the issue is less the building, and more the loss of that buildings' relationship to all the other buildings in the city.

interdependency problem

3/5

having no money causes tension and suffering from attachment, the Buddhist dukkha, because your persona, your "role" that you are in the other buildings has been impacted.

maybe he was known as a big swinger, wealthy, successful, cars, clubs, women

that's problematic

can you rebuild the downed building immediately? no, not an option, or at least not one which would restore his prior identities to 100%

so this attachment to these identities -- which are clearly unsustainable -- is going to be a source of everpresent pain and misery.

4/5

this is where "burn it all the fuck down" quietly enters the stage as a potential option.

it is a lever to be pulled once the pain becomes too intense.

you can see how he'd get there.

to resolve the tension, either the old building must go up, or the rest of the buildings must come down...period.

a man can be wealthy. a man can be broke. 

a man cannot be trapped in this phantasmagoria of bothness, between two semi-coherent yet nonexistent versions of himself.

he needs a new persona, new identity, needs to let the old "him" burn to the ground.

5/5

the much cleaner alternative is to just tell the world that he is officially dead-ass broke. men are simply too proud -- they'll never voluntarily choose this path.

would it solve all these problems, yes

but in doing so, there are so many interconnected identities, so many layers of shifting perception that he'd have to deal with along the way, a long road and an enormously painful one

people squawking the whole time, "did you hear he's getting evicted," "his lady left and took the kids," 

also, now that I think about it...it would not solve his problems at all.

it aligns his self-image (broke) with the world's perception of him. 

however, it doesn't signal an end...all it would do is begin the process of the other buildings being lowered or removed.

END: bad and worse

it also begins the public societal torture.

play by play humilitation

slow and drawn out, probably as painful as one could draw it up.

just a weak man getting vulture'd by his bad decisions, watching his old identity get dismantled bit by bit.

like choosing a voluntary pillory in the town square. 

the picture I am painting here, reality is probably 100x more painful, and there are 100x the elements to this that I haven't thought of.

so, burning it all down may go beyond pride. it may actually be the rational decision.

mostly because, the alternative is way worse than it seemed at first

you are going to lose a tremendous amount in both scenarios

neither seem to have significant moral/ethical upside or downside, screwed both ways

"I told the world the truth about myself" is not always wise, honest, or honorable, or at best its neutral. 
 
and for all we know, the slow road could take years, where you're in severe and glaringly public pain the entire time

or?

you can roll the dice with complete and total self-destruction

you self-immolate, and emerge as an identity yet to be determined.

I don't know which choice is "correct" - I just know which I've seen play out over and over.

**not investment advice

reminder

closure is a myth

one of those foolish notions that enters your head at a young age and is best squashed like a bug, asap, bc it does nothing but lead u astray + waste ur time.

1/5

expressed via dork behavior like “she dumped me, but I need closure, so I'm gonna text her until I get a reason”

brotha

u got the closure

when somebody tells u "its over," that means its over

permanently over in all possible scenarios

its hard to watch someone struggle with this reality, yet its also a position everyone has found themselves in once

there is no good outcome

if they come back in two days and say, "hey, actually, its not over"

you say: "no, it's over"

because the only other option is squid behavior and massive aura loss ("I'm so happy u kicked me to the curb, slept around, and now ur willing to take me back")

this rightfully makes them loathe you, so the 2nd "its over" is imminent

and now u are just destroying ur self-respect and dignity, chasing after someone who told u to get fucked.

don't do that, here are playbooks u can use.

2/5

dignity is less about their perception of u (they're history so who cares) and more about ur perception of yourself

u want to be automatic in the face of rejection

"u didn't get the job"
"it's over"
"u are fired, pack ur shit"

whatever lines and boundaries and principles u have, when they get crossed, all automatic

same reaction for everything

u can react in private on ur own time, but right now, u want to get to the point where its just...

"ok, see u later."

throw deuces and get the fuck out of there✌️

3/5

this will really fuck with people when u get it right -- which isnt the point of it -- but if u get dumped and can just shrug

or offer something like I've used: "well, its been real, it's been fun, it ain't been real fun."

and then boom, right out the door

they're sitting there like wtf

"did he ever care about me?"

now THEY need closure

but this is stupid petty behavior to not even think about or engage in.

u will make the mistake once, where u got in their head so bad, that they'll call u and u pick up. 

"can we talk things over?"

brief rebound, she gets closure -- "they are who we thought they were" -- and she dumps u again.

that's why when its over, its over forever.

4/5

u can always get your own self-closure

goal is, "never make the same mistake twice"

you want to figure out what parts of the mess were attributable to u.

its never 100% to 0%.

there is always some part u played in any broken relationship or job.

lets say its 50%-50%

you take that 50%, your 50%, and you take complete and total ownership of it.

you fix what is fixable, you eradicate any related defects of character so that it doesn't happen again, and then u move on.

u don't worry about the rest, that other 50%. its entirely out of ur control -- it doesn't exist.

5/5

in all these situations, u can melt down later in private

ur always gonna be shattered

there is no "just turn ur emotions off"

but I think u learn first in trading, then in life, that there are a lot of situations where there is no good outcome

there's down 20%, down 40%, and down 60%.

you take the 20% loss -- "good outcome, good process, best-case scenario" -- and move on.

this pattern is actually the sign of a very experienced trader/PM, they re-wired something, because it all goes against natural human instinct

factory install is 
1. "wait for the down 20% to rally to 0%, then exit."
2. "the good outcome is that she wants me back."

no. u are creating good outcomes and happy endings that do not exist...this is how the down 20% becomes down 60%.

is there an "upside" scenario?

that's why the goal in a lot of these, is just to escape with ur dignity intact.

u dont realize it, but u are in a bad/worse situation.

u will melt down in private over what happened

and if u handled it poorly, u will 2x melt down over "and then I made a fool of myself in front of everyone."

both are deserved. ur body is reacting as it should

the down 20% was there

u fucked around, u ate the down 60%, and u are feeling the sharp reproach of error, of shame, of cowardice, and of poor self-discipline.

the truth is that there is some upside scenario to all this

if u get blasted with horrible news, and people only see u stand up, wave goodbye and then walk out

when the dust settles, they're going to talk about how you took that shit like a G

u don't get a ton of these "true character" moments and so people always remember how it went down

"when the mask came off, he was actually tough as nails."

END 

this is why a man's final reaction in the face of death is so poignant, and inevitably becomes part of their story

Cicero "offering the neck" to his murderers, Cato pulling his guts out of his own stomach

Voltaire on his deathbed, so they say, was asked by a priest to renounce Satan...and responded with, "now is not the time for making new enemies."

this is why Montaigne writes about how many a wasted or debauched life, has ended up being redeemed by a noble death

so u may as well keep the few things they can never take from u

dignity, pride, self-respect

and "always die with dignity" is as good a name for this playbook as any.

been real, been fun

...but it ain't been real fun✌️

the "inner thorn" metaphor from Singer's Untethered Soul is extremely effective...common, visible, reliable way to think abt human behavior

u will watch a person's entire life form and take shape around a single motive: the desire to avoid something painful which lurks inside them...

was talking this over with a buddy

age as meaningless #, experience, jung's 1st/2nd half of life, "weeks where decades happen," severe life upheavals...pain risk wisdom, windows of opportunity

--

1/7

so the thing w/ his quote (40s are great, 50s u have a crisis), is that the age itself is sort of meaningless. 

one man's 35 is another's 40, or 45, or 50

it's not the age, it's that everything is driven by experience -- pain, suffering, failure

"there are decades when nothing happens, and there are weeks when decades happen" lenin

so... if you were to just lay on the couch for 20 years straight, from 30 to 50, not doing anything, u aren't magically granted some wisdom as the years pass

that's a falsehood to be dispelled bc I've gotten tweets like, "oh at 30 this happens, and 35 this happens," I might've said the same younger, idk

but if u do nothing, here's what happens: nothing

all u will do is decay.

2/7

whereas if u are 31 and u just go through it all in a single year, ur mind goes from 31 to 50 (in the best way possible)...experience is what makes someone seasoned and wise to the ways of the world

this dictates how ur friend group revolves, there are ppl who play it safe lifestyle-wise and there are people who take risk

paths diverge, u were on the same highway younger, now u just each took ur off ramp

jung's "1st half/2nd half of life" framework is prob the best

u will have friends who cross the plane (due to pain, experience), whereas others don't....idk if it's your choice

3/7

all the ppl I'm closest friends with, had their lives fall apart at some point in their late 20's or 30's or early 40's

lost all their $, divorce, drugs, lawsuit, jail, business failure

all the same personality type, high energy, high risk appetite...not the type to ever say "x happened to me," not sympathy seekers. just a part of ur nature + usually paired with, "the speed limit was 65, I should've been doing 75-80, I was at 100"

like u were just going at too fast a speed, for too long, where a bad outcome of some sort was due. 

and thats where u finally come face to face with ur own mortality, and thats when u shed the skin of ur 1st half of life and enter the 2nd half of life.

4/7

life goes on. ur new life is totally different from ur old life, but life goes on

and as time goes on, u see lots of other people, normal, quiet, God-fearing...who go thru periods of severe upheaval

they didn't even do anything wrong, like...u just get used to the fact that ur life, or anyone's life, can change, forever, in an single day. 

and the life u knew, is gone.

but out of the ppl I'm close with, every single person, if asked, "would u go back in time if u could and erase the actions + consequences"... says fuck no.

because u see who u are now, vs who u were then, and its like, are u kidding me, that guy wasn't built to be calm in chaos. he thought he was, but he wasn't.

and if u reflect on any of ur own errors or mistakes u will see its the same answer.  

everything u know about markets came from losing $...u cant go back and get the $, without giving up the experience/wisdom.

plus...the way I phrase it is that "fears melt away as they are faced head on."

nothing in life is ever as good as it seems, and nothing is as bad as it seems...pain is intense and short-lasting, and then u recognize the fear was always greater than reality.

and at a certain point u have made every mistake in the book, which has a massive positive impact on ur life

would u advise that someone go thru the consequences to get there...not intentionally. but dont live in fear either

and in this light, u recognize regret as silly and pointless in the self-pity/self-flagellation sense. just do better.

5/7

so that gets to the mcconaughey quote below which doesn't quite track

he says "40's were great but I see my 50's midlife crisis coming"

my buddy was like, "his 50-something, was my 30-something."

and that's what I said in the intro, and I agree

the comments on the 40s are dead on, but they usually come from someone who was just shipwrecked where u change ur life.

and hes setting expectations poorly for the majority of ppl who will inevitably have something turn their life upside down in their 40's, despite dodging the reaper so far.

6/7

once u understand that time ticks in linear fashion, whereas experience/wisdom come in massive chunks -- "weeks where decades happen" -- the way I see it, is that I want my experience to stay 10-30 years ahead of my age

my biggest concern is that I'm not dying enough deaths

you watch a year go by and compare the time elapsed vs the experience gain

and what would be a good year for most ppl, like, pain and failure sort of morph ur tolerance -- all for the better

ur level of risk, and ability to withstand pain, is now so much higher than normal and higher than what urs used to be. 

u notice it as hardship/adversity just sort of bounces off, and other people freak out over things where ur thinking, "u better pray nothing more major than this happens bc u are ill-equipped"

but each day that u do not die new deaths, or risk dying new deaths, whatever that means to u...is another day where the reaper closes the gap.

and ur age catches up to your experience

I don't have a crystal ball but when ur 80, I get the sense these moments and feelings are what u regret, far moreso than any mistakes u made.

the feeling of wasted time is never pleasant, ever

7/7

is this a good framework or one to mull over - unclear and it's out of my control. 

when ur gut, ur spirit talk to u, u listen.

it goes without saying to think for urself, never blindly take advice from any stranger on the internet or walk their path...shit might be fucked up, but work for them, but its not for u.

everything has to be unique to u, I'm merely here waving mirrors and lights around hoping it helps u see urself clearer.

I would frame mine if it resonates, in the healthiest light, as:

"I know where my ceiling is, I am nowhere near it...I'm not growing fast enough, I can handle a lot more discomfort/pain/risk than I am taking right now, and my lifestyle permits it."

and when all these things align, like, u gotta fuckin shoot.

thats what ppl don't get..."all clear" is the green light. 

there is no starting gun, only a window of opportunity, which remains open for God only knows how long.

its only when the light turns red, window slams shut, and and they're stuck, that they look back: "shit...the opening was there for 2 years, I was just being a pussy."

end

this is the answer that anyone will give u, to every and any question beginning with: "how do I know when its time to (take x risk)"

u never do, no one ever has....age old question, one I used to ask, always gonna be met with a shrug.

"motherfucker just went for it"

and thats 100% bw u and the man in the mirror...there's nothing on twitter for ya.

life isn’t "choose your own adventure," but it IS “choose your own gradient”

at all times you can adjust the difficulty level, the slope, the extent to which u live outside ur comfort zone, in each 24-hour block that we are allotted.

you can either push yourself on a daily basis, or you can never push at all.

make it as steep or as flat as you'd like...the truth is that its going to be hard either way.

many ppl run it at flat, when counterintuitively, flat may be the worst option.

first, because inertia and ennui become the challenge. they substitute for the degrees of the gradient, and they cause far more gloom and despair than any steep climb.

second, because once you reach the end of life, you look back across the flat stretch of land -- the gradient prairie -- and u realize that u never did any of the things you said you'd do.

"Some people die at 25," they say, "and we don't bury them until 75."

so while u cant control others, and u never want to go around telling ppl how to live their life

what u CAN control is who u surround yourself with. and far more important than a lot of the other shit people prioritize... is finding ppl who play the same game, on the same wavelength, and who approach each 24-hour block on the same gradient that you do.

10 random notes/compiled thoughts on greeks, stoicism, eternal issues, why these books should be read, and a healthy dose of "nothing ever changes"

--

what matters: these books are 2000 years old and have been read by every single generation of conquerors, warriors, heroes, and emperors

the modern-day narrative or associated individuals are gnats on a dog's ass

I feel compelled to put some distance here in ur mind...to disassociate whatever u have linked

if someone is humping a genre, and then they turn out to be a goober, you'll associate the genre with gooberdom

its understandable but flawed

"oh, you read the same books as ivanka trump"

like, that's not a thing. although I suppose it is, given the triggering it caused. 

what happens if Ivanka Trump reads the Bible, does everyone convert to Zoroastrianism

anyway...they are great books that have done a lot for me, these are random/assorted things I wrote down, and the article is similar

these books will outlive every one of us, no one could ever tarnish the old masters

some old books are hard to read. these really aren't.

1. Man to man across generations - thoughts from exile

most are literally just a man dumping his brain out...usually in hardship or exile or prison or shipwrecked or watching their kingdom burn around them

Dante's Inferno, while he was banished from Florence...all the best books were written from periods of extreme hardship or strife.

Seneca's letters to Lucilius are the best, again, written during exile

frankly, exile sounds kind of dope

"you must go live by yourself somewhere in northern italy, near Lake Garda....or, perhaps Ios, maybe Mykonos."

twist my fuckin arm

It all shows u that nothing ever changes, they had the exact same problems we do

Same for Juvenal, Horace, all these guys were sickos

Poems about "This Consul is off at his country house, and so here I am, fucking his wife."

I think the Romans have eight different words for fuck, you fuck someone in the mouth, the ears, the ass, they were really innovating in terms of where a dick could be placed

I'd like to say that we've made tangible progress on stuff like Nero on Capri, pools of young boys that he called his "tadpoles," but clearly sex pests and remote islands are a timeless theme. The only progress is we decree "you die now" versus "you are the emperor of Rome."

The best material though is on hardship and adversity, they really said everything that could be said, and nothing in the last 2000 years has surpassed it (esp Seneca)

2.  No one’s opinion matters

don't worry about what everyone else thinks

I don't like Meditations, it has the best PR team or some shit, but there are 5-10 better writers, wiser men, and so on

I keep going back and reading it and its one of those books I don't get anything out of

Plus the cuck-related aura loss is hard to shrug off

You're the Emperor of Rome, you can't be having gladitors screwing your wife...not the meditations you want to have

but again - these books are so damn old

there is no current day insight to add on what should be read

I would highlight anything Epicurus, Diogenes, Plutarch's Moralia....Lives of the Eminent Philosophers by Diogenes Laertius is a big compendium

and then Montaigne is a scholar who doesn't just quote them, he goes double-platinum...puts an entirely new banger essay on top of a 1500 year old banger essay.

Most of these are free online.

3. Plato/Socrates/Aristotle are mostly boring

again, fuck everyone else's opinion

Republic is readable, Nicomachean Ethics is somewhat readable, the rest can be tricky

so don't feel like you're dumb

Seneca's other book, Dialogues I think, is a better second step

the only people who have really read these other authors are Philosophy PhD's, it's that kind of material

everyone else is probably LARPing or trying to big-dick you on some shit they haven't read

if you pick a book up, and it sucks, put it away and pick up a new one. the good ones will grab you.

but with all these books, I want practical knowledge I can use...if it doesn't fit that bucket, or it's not history like a Tacitus/Thucydides, I don't really need all the science or the proofs of God

A lot of Plato's books are that kind of stuff

So you can respect that he was a great thinker, influential, while also saying "maybe its for you, its not for me"

ignore the crowd, form ur own opinion

4. modern translations suck

the "modern" translations are not a panacea, we've had english translations forever that were fine...a boring book is boring, and flowery language doesn't fix the issue

it just feels doubly wrong, like reading Cicero translated by a liberal Vassar grad

No one hated "effeminate men" more, Cicero would have veto'ed this on sight... "what have u done to my Tusculan Disputations, you wretch?"

he's up there in the sky hollering at Zeus... "sir, please, one more thunderbolt for this author -- I'm calling for Marc Antony's head on a pike, and I sound like Jane fucking Austen."

"I can't, I just used my last bolt on the Daily Stoic guy"

5. Trace ideas thru time

even a cursory read shows you what ideas are eternal

this helps you see through a lot of bullshit

a "new" idea thats actually 2000 years old, but no one reads old books

systems of goverment, a lot of ways we do things are a work-in-progress and its possible we've gone backwards

after 4800 years of monarchy and aristocracy, to think that 200 years of democracy is the endgame...

or that "love marriages" are ancient.  those are like 100 years old, the other 5000 years we didn't do that

have to always contemplate these ideas that are taken as stable, we really have no clue what we're doing

the people were never fit to govern themselves, ever...there may have been a reason for that.

we can tell them they're ruled by Louis XIV, or we can let them appoint their own kings and get Sneako and Nick Fuentes. 

Plus, the fourth turning is due, it's time for the "lets try communist/socialist policies" cycle which happens every 80 years like clockwork.

"here's 94 countries that have tried it. the record is 0-94."

"interesting. well...maybe this guy from Uganda can get it right?"

every 80 years the people who knew shit died, and we start fresh.

6. tune out of daily discourse

everything is a "new" argument over something we never have had an answer to, shit that the Romans struggled with.

immigration, crime, punishment, corruption, inequality, freedom, liberty

crime and punishment might be the most ancient out of all these discussions...prisons are 4000 years old, haven't changed the Old Testament

neither has punishment in general, we're less barbaric in our legal system, but humans are still bloodthirsty beasts -- no different than the gladiatorial combat days

but once you see how little has changed, you laugh at the big-brained takes, from elon or anyone else

"what if we had more public executions" - tried that. people still did crime. 

"what if we built more prisons" - interesting idea. we've tried it for 4000 straight years, and it hasn't worked. and while i'm not Plato, I struggle to see how the rational conclusion is: 

"we should keep doing more of what hasnt worked."

"okay...what if we put the criminals into the prisons BEFORE they do the crimes?" 

that would make sense, wouldn't it? 

just as a sanity check....do you think that occurred to anyone, at any point, since 1500 BC?

also, there's a few books that go into how this would work...1984, Huxley's books, Clockwork Orange

how do you feel about the government having a livestream of your brain at all times, and you go to prison when they detect the urge for criminal activity?

doesn't sound so good, does it?

that's why nothing has changed since the technicolor cloak. 

7. the rich

a consistent theme since the romans and greeks is that politicians and goverment figures are disgustingly corrupt, and have always been the "true" criminal class

that part hasn't changed a wink

the amount of securities fraud charges that elon himself has found a way out of will make a good book someday

tweeting "we're going private, funding secured"....that is straight to jail

unless you're a trillionaire

the truth is Elon's tweets aren't about the justice system, they're his way of broadcasting, once a day, to the 250 million followers, on the global app that he owns: "FYI, I don't like black people."

he switches it up, a mug shot, a guy who reoffended, a black judge, a tweet on "don't let them tell you it's racism when you're trying to save America"

keep in mind some 80 years ago we still had lynchings and segregated everything

I don't know, I guess after you make a trillion dollars you don't transform into Winston Churchill

the man is just about chasing e-girls, ambien, k-bumps and apartheid, and having 20 kids with 20 different women

at some point he'll let slip that all this space exploration is "because I just can't stand stinky, smelly minorities."

and then just when you think he's living clean he blasts out a "PARTY ON DRUGS" at 2 AM

what does it mean?

it's not from Seneca, that much I can tell you

8. all the stuff people suggest we do to solve crime is on LLM's, its all in the greeks and romans.

you just have to ask "have we tried X, and what happened"

there is nothing we haven't thought of

keep in mind we tied 4 horses to each of your limbs just for the fuck of it, we drag bodies through streets on chariots

the rich and the poor alike continue to gravitate to crime

"what if we executed the judges?"

the judge sentenced them 10 years ago and hasn't seen them since. why would you execute the judge?

"because the judge didn't know, 10 years in advance, what the guy was going to do when they got out....hmm, okay."

see, these all come back to almost comically dumb assumptions

"the judges are freeing violent criminals!"

ok, lets think this one through together.

Federal judges are a group known for their love of anarachy and chaos and disorder, they hate rules, they ignore precedent, they love standing out from the crowd and they love taking career-ending risks for no reason.

the only person I've seen doing interesting, thoughtful work on this as a concept is John Arnold

beyond that, some of the older ideas from the Romans may be worth bringing back, the colosseum, men fighting for their freedom...we aren't any better morally than we were then, we'd still enjoy watching people murder one another.

what about a 32-team playoff, 3v3, and the winning 3 gladiators get hired to do investment banking rotational programs at Goldman Sachs

"what's your greatest strength?"

"I just murdered 94 men with a dull Gladius, a broken spear, a scutum, and my bare hands."

"hmm...okay, we can probably skip the questions on how D&A flows through the cash flow statement."

9. immigration

some argue that immigration was the primary cause of the empire's decline

too many Greeks showed up, the populace got soft and heterogenous and patriotism declined, barbarians at the gate showed up (the RJR Nabisco deal), and Rome became a hub for high-yield debt issuance

hold on, I might have that wrong... "hallucinated," some would say.

anyway, whatever the greeks/romans said on races and religions mixing, it's probably relevant

demographics have always been destiny

I'm not sure it's what I want to hear -- because there are definitely parallels to the west today, and I stubbornly believe "can't we all just get along" is correct, rather than "lets just go back to having one race per country" -- but I'll listen regardless.

this just another one of those issues humanity can't seem to get right

a lot of other daily news and debates, you realize are just like a tape stuck on repeat

"how can we solve abortion, guns, states' rights, prejudice," et cetera

most are the same ideas as 2000 years ago and the same sides being taken

and so reading old books, u lose patience for a lot of shit and a lot of people

u hear nonsense being spouted off confidently, paired with ignorance

"new" ideas that were discredited or disproved eons ago

keep in mind we haven't figured out if red meat is healthy or not...it's only 200,000 years old, or something like that.

you know what would be worth figuring out at some point, is "why can't people get a good nights sleep?"

mars is nice, I think people would rather sleep though

what about carbs? do we have an answer yet? good carbs, bad carbs?

have we figured out protein? red wine? where are we on orange juice?

the reason is that these have been co-opted by lobbies, so we've lost the plot...for most of the 20th century, "studies" showed that sugar and coca-cola were wonderful for you

and milk, which I guess stopped paying the PR bill/bribe

losing interest in this shit is a good thing.

10. Temporal dislocation/mismatch -- Move laterally thru history

on old books in general, we are subject to a mental time warp

1600's feels ancient

have to stop and think about, around 1600, when Montaigne was writing about Seneca

...the book was 1500 years old.

so don't just think "pre 1900 = ancient" or that it's a different era, even these 200-300 year jumps or gaps tell you that something is timeless

and follow writers and thinkers from one book to the next

if Montaigne references Seneca a lot, read Seneca

if Seneca refrences Epicurus, read Epicurus

TR read Coleridge, Napoleon read Goethe, everyone had their sort of "man to man"

there's something to that....find comfort in what they found comfort in

u dont need new sources/secondary material, I haven't read the stoic guy's books (and I support the popularity of the material so I generally support him), but its just not necessary

the old ones are readable

some stuff u need secondary material (like a Nietzsche), but the Stoics didn't mince words

END. Seneca on current events

one hilarious thing is that Seneca probably would have hated the daily stoic guy

very low tolerance for building a career off someone else’s words - the bill always comes due.

"Put something forth from your own stock." direct quote of his

he would've hated Taleb too, quietly letting credit accrue to his name that he knows belongs to antiquity

the old heads were not a fan of dickriders, and they hated critics.  some shit is timeless.

so, its always better to be original and wrong

mix ur own words and experience in there as u stand on the shoulders of giants.

given the choice, I'd MUCH rather people call me weird than unoriginal.

I'm watching this Bessent tweet get engagement, there's like 4 comments "wtf is wrong with you"

what, can't a guy enjoy a trifecta character assassination?  shit, Seneca and Cicero would have loved that...especially around the Second Triumvirate, everyone talked so much fucking shit

Bessent just speedran the Phillippics

"Ceterum censeo esse delendam Alex Soros"

--

Conclusion: be yourself, everyone else is taken.

take risk, write something new, or at least try to come up with something new.

no more "here's 90% other people, with 10% me peeking through the bushes"

every time you put yourself out there,

you always get two comments in tandem

1. "that's the best thing I've ever read"
2. "what the fuck is wrong with you"

that's how it goes

humanity doesn't need another "how to improve your life in 4.23 seconds"

it will benefit more from another Infinite Jest

1000 pages of straight up insanity by a twisted mind who then took his own life

we need more of those. I don't know if I want to read it again, but I remember 100-200 pages of it being, like....wow, I thought I was demented.

don't kill urself after though, life is too good.

ave atque vale⚔️

Alright, so, this is such a good reply -- I'm surprised that no one else asked the same question.

"What if the stress is from family?" -- those are 100% some of the hardest fucking problems u will ever face in life

long post - I will try and break this all down.

"Be the bigger man" - 1/10

1. High-Level Shit

so, before getting into this, we gotta get square on beliefs

we may disagree. that's fine (and prob expected)

u can just recognize, these are the core beliefs that underpin the rest of this post.

It has taken me prob 5 years of heavy reading, trial and error, to get a functional system in place...it works...walk with me, keep an open mind.

if at any point u feel angry, exit

family is a "never argue w people" topic

too unique and we are all too poisoned mentally to be objective.

--

the top 2

some things u don't want to fuck around with, I would say top 2 are God and family

they are linked

blood is blood, loyalty is loyalty

u never turn ur back on family. u never cut anyone off.

there are very rare exceptions - assault, addiction - where they have to crash out/rock bottom...but then, u reappear and catch them.

so its only temporary, even worst case

if u believe in cutting family off, u can exit here - the entire post is predicated on not doing that.

we can politely disagree

but I am not fighting w/ anyone over that key point....thats why its up front

for ur own clarity, ask around, be aware of how the world and the crowd perceive a human that cuts family off

this isnt about me -- block/unfollow me, poof, I'm gone.

its about the 8 billion other people u have to deal with.

overall, the playbook for dealing w toxic people, doesnt work here. u are stuck with them (as they are with you) which is why stress is a major topic

2. Duty

as a man at least there is shit u have to do, whether u want to or not

to not do it, is to go against God

this includes taking care of ur parents and "being the bigger man" when they are totally out of line

forgive the past, they put up with ur shit

but, I'm pretty harsh on this topic w friends, w self, and in "top 2" topics, there is no point in mincing words

like, some parts of life have clearly defined right and wrong -- this is one of them -- so why fuck around.

when ur buddy is wrong u smack the shit out of him

3. Straight Talk

it happens, like guys get pissed at their 80 year old dad and block him out

but man to man, talking to u as I would a friend -- perhaps the ONLY person who is going to shit u straight

no way around it - brotha, u are dead ass fucking wrong, and u are being a petty little bitch-ass

there is shit u have to do, there is duty involved, and to not accept it puts u at the lowest of lows.

when I say God is involved, like, God will find a way to torture u for these decisions down the line, reminding u of times when u were pathetic or were a coward

call your fuckin mom and tell her u love her, today

tell ur dad u love him, ur grateful, whatever

if u have beef, dead it, forgive

fwiw, if reading this post is unpleasant for u, bail

this is the level I am at with friends and with self -- "real friends stab you in the front."

most people don't have one true friend who will slap the shit out of them

"ur fuckin dad is going to die soon, and when he does, God is going to put a burning spear thru ur heart. thats regret. it will be regret for the way u are acting right now, by not being the bigger man."

how do I know, mine died when I was young

and since then I've watched others make the same mistake u are making

u hold the grudge, they die, and u collapse..."what was I thinking"

"what I would give just to have lunch with him one more time...."

these are matters of God, mon frere....I am dead serious for a reason. the stakes are high.

4. Blood Loyalty

and then just in reading others...always ask

if u arent loyal to blood, who are u loyal to?

A: nobody.

I'm no-questions-asked out the door on that

"loyal to no one" is glaring, its reliable, and it can FUCK your life up if u dont understand the ramifications.

a man has never had a knife put into his back by an enemy

an enemy never gets a clean shot at your back -- u keep eyes on that motherfucker

the knife always comes from someone u let get too close.

so if I miss the 1 out of 100 who is a good dude, so be it...the other 99 are snakes or rats.

what is a man without family or loyalty?

just slithering around, using people to their advantage and discarding them when they're inconvenient

what u will learn is very simple

there is only one thing that happens when u hang around with snakes and rats:

u get bit.

many men are "not a friend and not an enemy."

that's what these are. nothings, avoids

pure opinion, but soon as u hear "I have no friends" or u sense "loyal to no one"...or ur gut says strange shit like "why are there no day ones"

there's something there

I get the message God, u only had to smash me with it 10, 15, 20 times.

and when u hear someone say over and over, "I'll die for my family," "x for my family,"

every man believes that, it doesn't need to be said.

when ur gut says: "he's smashing the gong a liiiiiittle too hard."

the depth of that relationship is millimeters, a dry twig

soon as u fart in the wrong direction, ur gonna get stabbed, with a "for my family bro"

slit ur throat for a nickel, "for my kids bro"

do a deal with them, what's normally a handshake, is direct to court. "u know how it is bro, I'll die for mine, its just biz, family first"

its not 100% wrong, sometimes its genuine -- its that most men have family AND friends

this is not an either/or

when its presented as such, listen to what is unsaid:

"if you put your faith in me, or invest too much into this relationship, you are going to learn a very painful lesson."

friendship is just not a thing for a lot of people

and they're telling u the deal. 

scorpion, frog, etc...they're not wrong, ur wrong for not listenening.

5. Nothing Is Special

people all have their "no I'm special" grudges and resentment

I'm not gonna convince u otherwise

ur situation isn't special...if u sent it out to Twitter, u would get laughed at for how juvenile it sounds (again, w/ very rare exceptions being violence, sexual assault, etc)

if ur gut says Twitter would dunk on u, listen to ur gut...means ur not being the bigger man.

u are just wallowing in petty shit...tom fuckin petty over there

"my 80-something year old dad said xyz and it pissed me off"

dude he's fucking 80

be the bigger man

how much shit did he go thru for you when u were a kid? guarantee it was worse than this

the stress is real, to answer the QT

I will get into exit strategies towards the end

for now, forgive forgive forgive

thats the counter for almost everything

example: "my dad was a piece of shit/bad father so I don't forgive him."

well....going through life without forgiving people and carrying vengeance, open sores, resentment, and being just a big angry pile of fire

your life is going to absolutely suck ass, you will never know peace

all part of the divine design

twtr has two camps, people trying to be helpful and upbeat, and then the people who are broken and toxic and pissed at the world...just lashing the fuck out at people, victim mentality

u are giving off camp 2 vibes

I can recognize instantly which camp someone is in...1, build, 2, block.

cars go 0 to 60, u want a "0 to block" time of two, three seconds

each second beyond that is an L. they win by wasting ur time

on camp 2, "never make the same mistake twice" has saved my bacon...but this one, I made the same mistake repeatedly

thinking that all men want to change, improve, climb, grow, build, succeed

they dont.

u can tell a man "here is exactly how to fix ur life" and they'll actively say, u know what, I'd rather stay down here than climb up there...they get more joy out of attacking people than their own success.

two men see ackman/pershing square
1st guy: "I'm gonna try and build that, so I can rise to his level."
2nd guy: "I'm gonna spend 50 years attacking him, so I can bring him down to my level."

that's how it is. scroll a guy's feed, u see immediately if he's 1 or 2....oil and water, ghibellines and guelphs.

cut, block, run

keep it moving.

6. Serve God

now..if u really hold urself out to be someone who seeks to know God, and imitate his ways

then u already know, u are not walking the walk.

at the heart of imitating God, is forgiveness, grace, kindness, mercy, love for family, and love for fellow man

emphasis: infinite forgiveness and infinite patience for family.

this is very important because I am going to just blast all excuses with that list

those are a pretty universal list of values, if your values don't align with those ("unforgiving, fuck people, fuck mercy"), like...I wish u the best but this post isnt going to help

get that hate out of ur heart.

again, if u arent on board with the "high-level" stuff so far (family, God) hit ESC

this is God territory in the sense that, family relationships hit emotions/feelings in a unique way

and when u go against this kind of shit, God finds a way to torture you internally...like betrayal of family/blood, idk if any deeper layers of hell exist

alright, lets do the tactics

7. Final Fantasy Tactics

ball knower video game

family situations suck ass.

family is aggravating, they cross the line and will say shit that is hurtful. happens to everyone.

you sit there, you suck it up, and u learn what it means to "set boundaries."

u dont cut people off, u let them know -- the line is here... if they dont respect it, the convo ends and u walk out

"when u are ready to be civil, come get me."

repeat until they respect your ground rules (which are mostly just basic respect)

"how do I deal with family stress?"

u just deal with it, because u put up with their shit, and someday, theyre gonna put up with ur shit.

family is all u got.

but u can minimize stress thru understanding boundaries -- if someone is being real fucking toxic or manipulative, there is the "stone face" response

"thanks for your feedback"

"thanks"

"I appreciate it and I'll keep that in mind"

not snarky, not sarcastic -- just, stone wall...this isnt a convo.

find something genuine that u would say. if its not genuine, u are escalating

passive aggressive/manipulator types thrive on this snarky/sarcastic back and forth

they're looking for u to take a subtle dig so they can ratchet the drama higher

u wanna make it clear...I am putting the fire out.

there's a lot of guys like this on twitter, just spending hours a day slipping subtle jabs, subtweets, passive aggressive remarks. extremely feminine

one woman in ur life is enough

u dont need men that act like women, trying to drag u into a cat fight

in life, its easier to cut/block/run

with family, the stone wall is u saying "not here - do that shit to someone else... u got the wrong guy."

once they see they can't get under ur skin, they move on

8. stress minimization

this is understanding how to put physical/emotional space between u and someone who is stressing u the hell out

and I'll assume its emotional stress, some stress is always normal...we're talking, u feel they're wrong-type stress.

u protect ur energy, u protect ur mental -- u have a life to live...if they are fucking with ur head, to where u cant work, cant sleep, cant function, thats really on you

because people are gonna do what they do. u cannot change that.

all u can change is how u react + ur coping mechanisms + self-respect + willingness to immediately pull up the castle gate bridge, like on a dime

"no, sorry, we aint doing that" - boom.

9. what do you believe?

if u dont have basic principles, this world will walk all over u...I didn't get this until my mid 30's

they are rules u keep with the man in the mirror, and no one, literally no one, crosses them.

if u are consistent, and u treat everyone the same, and always react the same to the same behavior...people WILL get in line.

if u bend, ur rules/principles are all worthless.

the go-to for dealing with stress, the mantra:

"BE THE BIGGER MAN."

breathe

u are right, they are wrong, happens a lot w/ family...emotions run hot.

but someone has to be the bigger man.

smile. say "thank you." 

look for the nearest exit

u can shake it off in private, just be the bigger man, quietly acknowledge "they're wrong and I just need to survive this interaction with my dignity intact."

it doesn't cure the stress, u will feel those barbs...but it will help re-align ur mindset/attitude and remind u who u want to be

stoic, basically

it hits u, u feel it, but u are able to quickly blunt the mental/emotional damage thru having a powerful mind, stocked with weapons and armor

and where u have cat-like reflexes in dealing with behavior or comments that are 100% wrong/toxic...just, "no"

10. mindset

ur gut instinct is literally the most accurate thing on earth in dealing with people. it understands concepts that we dont have words for.

I've been trading markets long enough where I have a pretty advanced relationship with it, but I wasn't sure if it applies better for life or for markets

its better for life. its human.

it feels the energy that people fill or drain from u.

the positive ppl are no brainers

if its neutral, bad, or even "good but sketchy"... trust your fucking gut instinct, my man

"why does this dude follow every girl I've ever slept with on social media, within minutes of meeting her"

heres the question u should really be asking

if u went to jail for a month and asked him "keep an eye on my girl, would ya"

what do u think would happen?

ur gut is telling u...u might just be stupid enough to want to find out the hard way.

"wow, I can't believe that snakes bite people. all the music/books/moves/tweets that said this would happen...it actually happened."

"I can't believe the guy that tries to fuck all my ex-girlfriends, wasn't a loyal dude"

brilliant insights dude... I hope u dont use that brain to cross the street

(in fairness, I said all these things at one point, which is why this post feels too close to home at times -- all learned the hard way)

no one ever says "hi, I'm a snake" or "a rat" or "hi, I'm a fake friend!"

you hear about them constantly though

most people learn what a rat is, they have a friend who was doing dirt, he got caught, and to get a reduced sentence...says u were the kingpin, and testifies against u.

the first glimpse is your best friend, on the stand, trying to get you 120 months so he can get probation instead of 5

thats just one of many scenarios but it illustrates the same point

"its never ur enemies that get u, its always ur own people"

END

at a younger age this isnt intuitive, and its why family will inflict deep wounds on u... u dont understand yet that theres a balance

u sit there and let them fuck you up and ruin your entire day, for no reason other than misguided loyalty

touches on 10 random things:

1. quote is like the one from Baltasar Gracian: 

"When one enters into the house of fortune by the gate of pleasure, one leaves it by that of sorrow, and vice versa."

2. the duality of all things.

nothing is as good as it seems, but nothing is as bad as it seems, either...u get it both ways.

and then the relationship/connection/interplay between pain and pleasure -- the removal of todays pleasure, will be what constitutes tomorrow's pain

one of those glaring realities of human nature - u get nothing for free, ever

3. the "harshest defeat"

like what spinoza wrote about how a friend that becomes an enemy, is a far more bitter foe than if the friendship had never existed in the first place.

similarly, the most violent hatred you will ever witness, always existed first in the form of love.

4. losses follow wins

partially as balance, and partially because the W itself was what created the L. 

"Success is a poison that should only be taken late in life and then only in small doses.” - Trollope

alternatively, losses restore equilibrium...the opposites emerge at the poles + duality reigns supreme:

"Prosperity doth discover vice, as adversity doth discover virtue." Bacon

5. sardonic tone

not the perfect word but I get his drift

its the gentle, cynical mocking that becomes instinctual in the face of joy...recognizing that it never lasts, it's all fleeting

you acquire this after massive shifts in fortune, peaks and valleys, pride and shame

and u develop the sage's mix of contempt and apathy for human nature, in all its infinite vanity

the tone is that of Pascal, or Schopenhauer, or Montaigne's essay "Democritus and Heraclitus"

it's never in a bitter way...sardonic is slightly off, more melancholic and amused, but not quite at contempt and scorn

all part of ur very brief tour of planet earth.

6. there is only one fixed and immutable presence 

the sole presence that is guaranteed to be with u from the cradle to the grave. 

that presence is God.

beyond that...everyone and everything in ur life will leave you someday.

they will either leave physically, or they will leave thru death.

7. you accept this impermanence with a warm heart

and u enter new relationships with eyes wide open. nothing changes. u are always receptive to joy, to pleasure, and to love, and u are always willing to risk your heart.

but simultaneously, u are silently laughing to urself. because u must always ponder the balancing act, visualizing the negative scenario

contemplating, at the dawn of a promising new relationship: "man, I cannot fuckin WAIT to see how this one ends."

have to laugh at all of this, and let it roll off ya

8. there is a balance here between pessimism and warmth

its very rare in a human - "old soul" types that are decades wiser than their age.

most people are naive/optimistic/unwilling to face harsh realities. not enough risk, not enough failure, not enough pain...same mindset & attitude as 20 years ago.

others go too far in the other direction and become broken, bitter, resentful, cruel, hateful, envious "victim mentality" types.

those are the extremes to avoid.

9. there is a term from Leopardi, "the courage of philosophical pessimism"

where he cautions, don't attribute my pessimistic outlook to my demeanor or temperament or circumstances...I arrived here through research.

Tolstoy's "Confession" is another good case study, a man on a similar journey to what is being described here -- the emptiness explored by Schopenhauer, King Solomon, Buddha -- and then going the other direction, away from intellectual pessimism, and towards the simple Russian peasant's belief in God...the same final destination every sage and philosopher arrives at.

but that's what the discerning eye can pick up on -- bad negativity/pessimism vs acquired realism + a willingness to call balls and strikes, starting with urself.

the untrained eye just sees something dark, grim, emotionally distant, disturbed, and chalks it up to "circumstance made them that way"

a way to frame it: those who understand and face Jung's "shadow," and those who don't...the 1H/2H dynamics, stuff that Jung disciples like Rohr write about.

go to my pinned tweet, ctrl+f Jung, read parts 1-2.

10. the final goal

you want to develop fluency in suffering, and be fearless and courageous in confronting all the ugliest sides of life...but u don't want to let ur warm heart turn cold in the process.

I cannot give u step-by-step directions on how this is done, mostly because I think 100% of any calibration has been against my will.

the pain/suffering that shape u, and push u towards final form, are involuntary by definition.

the naive archetype remains naive bc avoidance of pain is the primary objective.

but without pain, there is no growth and thus the mind stagnates.

(END)

at some point u have to take a risk, one where there is a real possibility that u are left shattered on the ground, covered in blood and broken glass.

without that risk, there is no chance of progress.

I wish there was a more pleasant answer, but that's reality. u really see it from ages 20 to 40, the people who change and shift and grow and mature...almost entirely a function of pain and suffering.

c'est la guerre

do with this information what u will...and recall:

joseph campbell: "the cave you fear to enter, holds the treasure that you seek."

lots of good commentary on this intvw, I have very little to add except highlighting this one clip re: lollapalooza effects

on modeling px/vol/margins + translating qualitative input to quantitative output

putting aside the bull/bear debate or the man in question -- generally if dan loeb says someone is "one of the smartest and savviest investors he's ever met" u can prob disregard the peanut gallery -- this is the right way to think about a business transformation/narrative shift

u can basically follow his logic line item by line item, or from top-down to bottoms-up:

-what is mkt share / has it changed / what is industry growth rate
-what is unit growth %
-what is ASP growth %
-what's the new GM% profile
-then flow that onto a fixed cost base/degrees of op leverage

this framework is always behind any story where EPS goes from 20 cents to like 20 dollars

I dont think u see variant views of this magnitude outside of tech....the same dynamic/flow-thru exists re: px/vols/profitability, but just much lower delta vs street ests (thinking consumer + industrials)

and then last, the way he frames visibility + duration of supranormal growth, is how you'd think about the multiple/disc rate in a DCF.

combine it all and u get the "lollapalooza effect" in action.

I loved this episode between @patrick_oshag and Alex Sacerdote. Probably one of my favorite investing podcasts of all time. For my way of thinking and investing, this was an A+ 💯. 

As I was nearing the end of the episode, I thought to myself "Alex has mapped out the entire global tech stack and ecosystem and uses that map as his guide to the future.” As soon as I was thinking of that, Patrick said that Alex has "built a research machine to understand the world through the lens of companies.” I think it's the same thought, just different way of saying it.

Alex also gives a nice shout-out to @shaunmmaguire who was talking to Alex about the opportunities in hardware three years ago.

Here are some of the quotes I am filing away…

“Anytime you have a new compute paradigm, there is a new [tech] stack, and that creates new winners and losers on the old stack.”

“We have this infrastructure layer S-curve, which we think is like 10% penetrated, and by the way, we think it’s still one of the best ways to play Ai.”

“Sundar said its 10 basis points of the knowledge workers in the world [currently using Ai coding tools].”

“We think the enterprise application Ai market is less than 1% penetrated. We talk about S-curves, but we call this an L-curve.”

“We’re at 10 basis points of people really using Ai and we’re already sold out of compute…there’s not enough compute in the world.  So, Anthropic has half of what they need right now.”

“We do 2,000 to 3,000 face-to-face meetings with management teams each year, and about 10% to 15% of those are with privates.”

“We have an investing framework of (1) S-curves, (2) competitive advantage, and then (3) underappreciated earnings power…when you get the right part of the S-curve you get exponential unit growth if you have a very strong business model (which in tech there are so many of those for so many different types of moats), your earnings don’t grow linearly, they grow exponentially, and that is the last piece…invest when there is underappreciated long-term earnings power, and very often the earnings can grow from $1 to $10 or 50 cents to $20, and it happens way more than you think, and it allows you to buy some of the best companies in the world for extremely low P/Es. When we were buying Nvidia in 2023, we were paying 4x earnings. When we bought Tesla in 2019 for the car S-curve, we were paying 5x earnings. When we were owning Apple, we were paying 4x earnings. When we bought Amazon for AWS we were getting it for free.”

[Fascinating about how the bottom part of the S, before the exponential growth phase, can last 10+ years]: “Smartphones were out ten years before the iPhone. The Internet was out 20 years before Netscape…Tesla went public 15 years before 2019 when it went vertical.”

“Andy Grove says when you have strategic inflection points you can’t trust the data. Strategic inflection points are about intuition, anecdotal evidence.”

“BTW, it’s OK to be late. It’s OK to miss the first one, two, three years in a lot of cases because if the top of the S-curve is half a trillion, the growth can go on for a long time. It’s OK to miss the first 100%.”

“I started at Fidelity and Peter Lynch loved to mentor young kids, so I got some time with him, and he said “whiteout the chart. It’s all about the future.”

“First we look at the S-curve and then we do an exhaustive study of everyone with exposure in that area and try and find the one with a very powerful competitive advantage.”

“Warren Buffett didn’t like tech because he couldn’t predict the future. But the S-curve is our map for looking into the future.”

“We sold almost all of our application software…entering this year we were actually net short [SaaS].”

“You can imagine a world where in one, two, four, five years you could have a brand-new AI native company going after each one of these very strong [SaaS] incumbents.”

“In software there is the Rule of 40…for chip investing we have a new Rule of 40: what percent of your sales are AI and what is your market share in that category (say 30% and 30%, you’d be 60%...that’s a great place to look because you’ve got exposure and you’ve got a strong market position). The problem with software is their AI is 1%-2% of sales and it’s a long way to go.”

“AI could make some of these software platforms more important because what’s the first thing you do with Claude??? You plug it into Slack.”

“The workloads in AI are growing 10x every year. And it is pushing every single aspect of hardware to the physical limits of what it can do. So not only are you creating tremendous unit growth, but we are experiencing the de-commoditization of the hardware industry. I met with Shaun Maguire like three years ago and he said I wish I could come back and be a hardware hedge fund because all the companies are public, and they all have powerful IP…and we’re in this renaissance of chips so not only do you have tremendous unit growth but it’s requiring tremendous innovation across every aspect of the server and so…”

“We need you for the next four years designing this road map with us.”

“No one has paid attention to hardware and chips at all. So, we’ve got all these newbies coming into it.”

“One thing that bothers me is there is a lot of negativity in the general population about AI. And there is a lot of negativity in some aspects of the government…But I do think that the genie is out of the bottle. Another risk is that if AI slows down in its improvements…then the open-source models will catch up and then it could be a race to the bottom and it wouldn’t be good for the stocks, probably…it could be good for the chip companies because chip companies don’t care who wins.”

“We’re meeting with as many companies as humanly possible…the [scuttlebutt] system we use is right out of Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits by Phil Fisher.”

“Phil Fisher said get to know ten or fifteen like-minded people [investors] around the country and share ideas…you share ideas and it’s important that it’s a two-way street. I call it the tripod when I like something, and then my analyst like it, and then somebody who I really respect also likes it. Those three legs of the stool can really help the conviction.”

“We think there is a huge structural underweight of the largest tech companies in the world…[partly because] there is a belief that there is no alpha in large caps]…[investors worry there is not alpha in big companies] but we realized this is just a product of the digital economy in that in tech the leader usually grows bigger and wins and develops very high market share quickly and there is great competitive advantages, and they are also selling around the globe so this is going to lead to massive profit pools and massive market caps…And most endowments are betting against this because they are completely underweight this…I think there is tremendous alpha in the largest cap because with a small cap it takes just one person to figure out it’s good and move it up. But it takes 100 diversified PMs to realize Google is not a loser, it’s a winner, and can we figure that out before 95% of those generalist PMs?…and we’ve been able to do it and we like our odds on that.

Disclosure: I am an investor in and the portfolio manager of the Bastion Industrial and Infrastructure portfolio, which owns shares of Nvidia, Alphabet, and Amazon. I personally own shares of Apple and Tesla.

quotedTweet.text:
the 10 best books/resources to learn fundamental equity valuation and markets

plus some books/authors that didn't make the cut and why they were excluded

--

(1/4) - INTRO

so I have a list in my pinned tweet with a bunch of books/series/intvws

its brief by design (30 ish names) - expectations investing, market wizards, mauboussin, snowball, stuff like that

sometimes I get questions "why isnt xyz on there" (someone just asked about Soros' Alchemy of Finance)

I will give my opinion (and thats all any of this is, opinion) as to why some names are were excluded

keep in mind this is directed at someone with 0-10 years experience. after 10+ then I suppose anything is "in play" (ie Alchemy of Finance), but theres no point in reading titles like that w/o having Buffett/Mauboussin down cold

--

(2/4) - TOP 10 / DO NOT PROCEED UNTIL FINISHING THESE

1. Mauboussin - expectations investing

2. mckinsey on valuation

(dull, but this is as close to The Bible as we've got for fundamental equity valuation. there is stuff in here that will pop up time to time where its not "mission critical" but where someone will look at u like...um really? so u want a passing familiarity at the minimum).

3. Mauboussin (total compendium)

go to his page, michaelmauboussin dot com, then go to Writing. obviously there are REAMS of content here, but its similarly Biblical to McKinsey, except more readable and does a better job linking to how mkts actually trade

I've been trading mkts since 09 and I still go read mauboussin notes all the time and find new insights in them.

4. buffettfaq dot com

also the BRK letters, which can be dull, fall under "constantly," meaning, you can proceed without going top-to-bottom, but keep reading these + Mauboussin in ur spare time

again, as with mauboussin, since 09 I still read BRK letters (on brks website) all the time and find new insights in them.

5. Market Wizards + New Market Wizards + Hedge Fund Market Wizards

idk about any of the series after that...you'll lol when you look at the original "Wizards" (its like Druck and PTJ) relative to the newish ones... I'm not gonna throw shade, u can see for urself.

and the critics are correct to point out that without including audited track records for a 2026 "wizard," the crowd is going to call bullshit. we dont need Bruce Kovner's track. we do need it for Twitter Substack Wizards or Wizards of Seeking Alpha or whatever these new collections are called. 

6. Snowball (on buffett)

7. Poor Charlie's Almanack

8. Spend a lot of time on Graham & Doddsville (columbia b-school newsletter), the ones from 2010-2020 had some REALLY good investors on there with great intvws - lot of the storied tiger cub PMs.

as with market wizards, I havent recognized a G&D interviewee in at least six years...not throwing shade, but like, u dont gotta tell me who Lee Ainslie is, u do have to explain "heres a guy who finished MBA in 2024"

9. Spend a lot of time on VIC going thru old pitches. Sort by all-time, highest ranked, spend years on this.

10. Read Ed Chancellor's books esp Capital Returns + Capital Account

Honorable Mention: Lynch/Fisher/Jesse Livermore. Also 25iq dot com, by Tren Griffin, is an awesome collection of investor wisdom, as is mastersinvest dot com.

--

(3/4) NOT ON THE LIST

1. Damodaran. He's worth reading, but overly academic to me...way too far away from how markets actually trade. His DCFs are sound academically but its always like "TSLA is at $1450, but based on my assumptions, its worth $12."  

Like, brotha, ur DCF is missing something lol. Maybe tsla is worth $1000, or $2000, or even $750, but the lack of understanding the stock's narrative is what overly-academic practitioners miss.

I'd still read what he writes - I put him #1 because I want it to be clear, he is as sharp as it gets on academia/theory -- just pay attn to Mauboussin's writing vs his and you'll see what I mean.

2. Taleb. I am not throwing shade but go back and read the Greeks, there is nothing he has said that they didnt cover already - I'm not blaming him, its just a misconception by the readers.

Like referencing a term "ah yes, thats like Taleb's xyz." No, thats Aristotle, or Juvenal (black swan), or Procrustes (greeks), like, the idea that you have to read these as part of a market education is incorrect.

Taleb is highly intelligent and I'm assuming he acknowledges his sources, and I always appreciate a sharp brain that can link old concepts to new ideas (the stock market). So I'm not attacking him personally. This is strictly a "do equity analysts need to read this book" and the answer is no.

3. Soros

this guy's stuff is unreadable to me. I'm pretty stupid, but I recognize dense writing when I see it. you can be both brilliant and a bad writer at the same time.

I have nothing but respect for him as a money manager, he's one of the GOATs. but to learn markets, I mean, you might get one or two good insights from 300 pages of his writing, its just very obtuse

by way of comparison, buffett is both brilliant and a great writer. a genius takes the complex and ELI5's it. a book that is brilliant yet unintelligible is a bad book.

4. Housel

Okay, so, I worship Housel. He should probably be read. He is the fucking man, I have watched his career since 2013 or so when he had no followers and was writing for Motley Fool. 

My immediate reaction was "this guy is one of the best financial writers I've ever seen," and it has been a pleasure to watch him ascend and then bang out a book that has sold 10 gorillion copies. 

Young guys, pay attention, this is how you launch a career off twitter.

Only reason I didnt include him is that I feel like he aims more towards a casual/hobby investor, not a fundamental equity analyst which is who this list is aimed at. 

There is probably a separate list for Housel's category - "How to think about money and markets in general," aimed more at the man on the street. Someone should do a top 10 for that, mine would just be 1. Housel 2. ask Housel for the rest of the list.

Either way he's one of our generation's premier talents in writing about markets, he absolutely has a gift.

5. Ben Graham/Greenblatt/Klarman

Security Analysis is boring as fuck and its okay to admit it. As for the Greenblatt and Klarman books, they're good, but anything "Value Investing" can be deferred/delayed.

the reason is that value investing has been dead for 15 years or so, I dont know why. it'll come back, it always does, people can dunk on Einhorn all they want but he is correct in that value investing is backed by academia/theory/historical perf as a strategy that works.

practically...theres no point in learning "Net Nets" when none exist anymore (or at lesat right now), its like this strategy got arbed out or something. 

I'm not saying "no," I'm saying "go read BRK/Mauboussin instead" - u dont have infinite time.

"but theres net-nets in all these foreign countries" - yeah, there are. and you'll figure out why as soon as you start fucking around with them. 

markets are far too competitive for u to just say "oh wow a $150M company with $160M in cash, free lunch!"

caveat investor

6. Howard Marks

I like him, but the critics are correct. His books/memos are just platitudes...."You should be optimistic, but exercise caution, and always think about reward relative to risk."  Useful if u have questions like "is it sunny in the summer?"

similar to Greenblatt/Klarman/Soros/Graham, there are absolutely a few good nuggets in a 300-page book, but again, we're speaking in Return on Time terms. one Berkshire letter or mauboussin piece = 99.9% of investing books.

7. all the "History" books

tons of these, Madness of Crowds, Barbarians at the Gate, Michael Lewis, A Random Walk, shit like that

worth reading, yes, but not until you've mastered the fundamental shit. again, the "actionable insight per 300 pages ratio" is just not good.

plus sr's and ur boss will just look at you with disdain if you get too, like, "ah yes this current market backdrop is like the 1613 Dutch Tulip Crisis/South Sea Company!" like bro stfu and build the fucking model we hired you to build lol

8. Macro books

there's some books like Volatility Machine that I loved, but for a fundamental equity analyst, you do not need to spend your precious hours (at least at first) learning this stuff

the plumbing of foreign sovereign debt markets, why argentina keeps defaulting, the tequila crisis/mexican peso de-peg

its really interesting, but just not all that relevant....none of this would ever be in a stock pitch

--

(4/4) - END

I think that's it. If you disagree with the top 10, and think a certain title deserves a spot in there relative to one that I have, I'm all ears...the goal is to get the 10 right.

On the non-top-10, please dont argue, I'm not shitting on those people. Nor is there any point to repyling, "heres ten other books I enjoyed," because thats how a guy ends up with 1250 bookmarked titles and doesnt read any of them.

there are TONS of "marginal" finance books. I've read them, you've read them, we don't need a compendium of those.

The goal is to figure out the absolute best books - the ones where for the rest of ur life, if someone asks "what do I read," you know exactly what to say:

"read these 10 books and do not read anything else until you have mastered these." 

because people will actually read those 10.

--

good luck reading
